meta.title: LPKF Laser & Electronics — Klaus Fiedler's laser micromachining pivot through LIDE glass processing and semiconductor advanced packaging
meta.abstract: LPKF Laser & Electronics SE (LPK.DE on Frankfurt Xetra) is a German specialty laser systems company focused on laser-based precision micromachining for electronics, automotive, and emerging applications. The strategic narrative through 2024-2026 has centered on the LIDE (Laser Induced Deep Etching) glass processing technology for advanced semiconductor packaging substrates including glass core substrates emerging as alternative to organic substrates in AI accelerator packaging contexts, plus the broader PCB prototyping and laser welding systems business.

chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
The forward strategic narrative at LPKF Laser & Electronics centres on glass. Specifically, the company's proprietary LIDE (Laser Induced Deep Etching) technology — a two-stage process combining ultrafast laser modification of glass with selective wet etching to produce through-glass vias and precision deep features — is positioned as the enabling tool for the semiconductor industry's gradual migration toward glass core substrates in advanced packaging. That optionality, not the company's legacy PCB prototyping or plastic welding revenues, has driven the most intense investor interest heading into 2026, even as the underlying business navigated a difficult contraction in its fiscal year.

LPKF trades on the Frankfurt Xetra Prime Standard under the ticker LPK.DE. The company was briefly added to the SDAX ~~and TecDAX indices~~ ==index== in December 2024, only to be removed in the December 2025 periodic review — a reflection of its small-cap profile amid broader index rebalancing. Headquartered in Garbsen, near Hannover in Lower Saxony, LPKF was founded in 1976 and built its initial franchise on precision circuit-board prototyping systems before expanding into laser direct structuring, solar cell scribing, and laser plastic welding over subsequent decades. Dr. Klaus Fiedler has served as chief executive since January 2022; the supervisory board extended his contract through December 2028 in April 2024, signalling confidence in the strategic transformation underway.

## Four Segments, One Strategic Pivot

The company's four operating segments — Development, Electronics, Solar, and Welding — each carry distinct demand dynamics. Development encompasses PCB rapid-prototyping tools and laser direct imaging systems sold to electronics research labs, universities, and defence contractors; it performed resiliently through 2024-2025, underpinned by sustained North American demand before a brief disruption from U.S. government procurement delays in Q4 2025. Electronics covers laser depaneling systems, molded interconnect device structuring, and the growing cluster of LIDE-adjacent glass substrate systems. Solar reached record revenue exceeding €40M in fiscal 2024 as LPKF briefly became market leader in thin-film laser scribing for CIGS and CdTe modules, only to see order intake collapse in the second half of 2025 as the segment's customers deferred investment amid an incomplete technology transition toward perovskite architectures. Welding — serving automotive, medical device, and consumer electronics assemblers — absorbed a roughly 20% revenue decline in 2024 as automotive capital spending contracted.

## Financial Trajectory: Contraction Before Potential Inflection

Consolidated revenue fell to €115.3M in fiscal 2025, missing the company's ~~own guidance of €125–140M~~ ==original €125–140M guidance while meeting the low end of the updated €115–125M range,== and declining from €122.9M in fiscal 2024, as Solar's second-half collapse overwhelmed solid performances in Development and pockets of Electronics. Adjusted EBIT improved marginally to €0.8M (0.7% margin) from €0.1M the prior year, but reported EBIT was negative in both periods. Order intake fell a more alarming 19.9% to €91.6M, compressing the backlog to €27.1M — nearly half its year-earlier level — as customers across Solar and portions of Electronics deferred commitments. [LPKF FY2025 results press release](https://www.lpkf.com/en/news-press/press-releases-teaser/lpkf-reports-slight-improvement-in-earnings-in-2025-and-initiates-group-realignment)

For fiscal 2026, management guided revenue of €105–120M and an adjusted EBIT margin ranging from −3.0% to +4.5%, explicitly assuming significantly lower Solar revenues. The first-quarter print confirmed pressure: revenue fell 32% year-on-year to €17.1M and adjusted EBIT was −€5.7M. The constructive signal was a book-to-bill ratio of 1.4 on order intake of €24.1M, a 17.6% increase over the prior-year quarter. [LPKF Q1 2026 press release](https://www.lpkf.com/en/news-press/press-releases-teaser/lpkf-gets-off-to-a-solid-start-in-2026)

In September 2025, the company launched the "North Star" restructuring programme, consolidating welding and solar system production from Fürth to Suhl and targeting double-digit EBIT margins by 2028 across a leaner operational footprint.

## LIDE: Commercial Signals, Not Yet Commercial Scale

LIDE progress in the period has been incremental but directionally positive. In December 2024, LPKF disclosed an ad-hoc order for LIDE systems for series production in the display sector — the first production-scale commercial win — valued in the "mid seven-digit euro range" with delivery commencing immediately and continuing through 2025. [EQS ad-hoc filing, December 13 2024](https://www.eqs-news.com/news/ad-hoc/lpkf-receives-order-for-series-production-with-lide-in-the-display-sector/b13f7624-08db-406d-af36-35ae5962c4c2) In Q2 2025, Onto Innovation installed metrology equipment inside Vitrion — LPKF's own glass processing foundry in Hannover, which functions as a customer qualification facility — as part of Onto's packaging applications centre of excellence. [Onto Innovation / LPKF PACE press release](https://www.lpkf.com/en/news-press/press-releases-teaser/onto-innovation-and-lpkf-are-set-to-accelerate-mass-production-of-glass-core-substrates-for-semiconductors) In October 2025, LPKF delivered LIDE equipment to Fraunhofer IZM's Glass Panel Technology Group, a fifteen-company consortium developing large-format glass panel substrate and redistribution layer processes. [Fraunhofer GPTG press release](https://www.lpkf.com/en/news-press/press-releases-teaser/lpkf-delivers-key-strategic-technology-to-fraunhofers-glass-panel-technology-group) Supply-chain analysis suggests LPKF equipment is in use or qualification at Samsung Electro-Mechanics, UTI, and Unimicron, though LPKF does not confirm customer names. The Korean Patent Office granted new LIDE patent protection in September 2025 covering the company's "earthworm structure" — a specific through-glass feature geometry central to via formation in thin glass substrates. As of Q1 2026, Fiedler described LIDE systems as "in use by numerous semiconductor customers in test and R&D environments," with production-order inflection projected around 2027.

> "We are consistently evolving from a machine supplier into a provider of functional solutions with disruptive technologies, clearly focused on growth markets." — CEO Klaus Fiedler, Q1 2026 earnings statement

## What This Dossier Asks

The central question for LPKF is timing: whether LIDE glass substrate demand converts from engineering qualification and one-off display orders into recurring semiconductor packaging production orders before the company's structural cost reduction programme has repaired the core business enough to sustain the investment. Secondary questions involve the competitive position against Belgian rival LASEA and other laser micromachining specialists, the durability of the Development segment amid shifting U.S. and European defence and research procurement, the Solar segment's path toward a perovskite-era product cycle, and the Welding unit's ability to return to profitability under the Suhl consolidation. Each segment thread is examined in the chapters that follow.

chapters.title: From 1976 founding through laser micromachining specialization to LIDE
chapters.body:
## Workshop to Photons: ~~Erlangen, ~~1976

LPKF Laser & Electronics began not as a laser company but as a maker of circuit-board routing machines. ~~Founded in 1976 in Erlangen, Bavaria — a university city already developing an identity as a hub for electrical engineering —~~ ==Founded on August 4, 1976,== the company's initial proposition was unglamorous but commercially durable: allow electronics engineers to prototype printed circuit boards in-house, without waiting days for a chemical etching house to return results.

Early LPKF systems were mechanical — carbide milling spindles cutting copper-clad laminates under microprocessor control — and the value proposition was speed. An engineer who needed a revised PCB layout could have a working board in hours rather than days. That cycle-time compression, modest in absolute terms, was transformative for product development workflows across automotive electronics, industrial controls, and the nascent personal computing industry.

~~The business relocated north to Garbsen, near Hannover, as it scaled through the 1980s, establishing~~ ==The business moved to its Garbsen headquarters near Hannover in 1991, establishing== the Lower Saxony home it retains today. The move placed LPKF within reach of northern Germany's dense automotive and electronics supply chains, a proximity that would later prove advantageous as laser welding and antenna structuring businesses matured. The company listed on Frankfurt Xetra under the ticker LPK.DE, ~~eventually earning inclusion in the SDAX index — a measure of mid-market recognition rather than scale, for the revenue line would remain in the low-to-mid triple-digit euro millions across most of its public history.~~ ==briefly joining the SDAX index from December 2024 to December 2025 — a marker of mid-market recognition rather than scale, since the revenue line would remain in the low-to-mid triple-digit euro millions across most of its public history.==

## Milling to Photons: The Laser Inflection

The shift from mechanical to laser-based processing was not instantaneous. LPKF integrated laser technology progressively through the 1990s, first as an adjunct to mechanical systems and later as the primary modality. Laser direct imaging — ablating copper and dielectric layers with controlled pulses rather than milling with a carbide bit — offered step-change improvements in feature resolution and eliminated tooling wear, a chronic cost and reliability issue in mechanical routing.

The flagship product line that emerged, the ProtoMat series, became a category standard in laboratory PCB prototyping worldwide. Universities, R&D centres, and tier-one electronics manufacturers purchased ProtoMat systems as standing development infrastructure — a recurring-revenue base that made LPKF's core Development segment resilient through multiple industry downturns. The ProtoMat and associated ProtoLaser platforms defined what the company would formalise as the Development segment: low-volume, high-mix board production without the capital commitment of photolithographic processing lines.

By the early 2000s, LPKF had accumulated a global installed base of several thousand systems in this category, a commercial position that provided both stable revenue and a customer-relationship network seeding future product introductions. The Development segment would prove the company's most consistent cash contributor even as the grander ambitions of subsequent eras rose and fell around it.

## Laser Direct Structuring and the Antenna Dividend

The most commercially significant technology LPKF originated in its own laboratories was Laser Direct Structuring — LDS. The process allowed designers to mold three-dimensional plastic components and then use a laser to activate a metal-organic additive embedded in the plastic, creating a pattern onto which copper could be electrolessly plated. The result was a three-dimensional circuit trace formed directly on the surface of the molded part, eliminating the rigid flat PCB substrate entirely for applications where geometry permitted.

LDS became commercially material at precisely the right moment: the smartphone explosion of the late 2000s and early 2010s created insatiable demand for compact, high-performance antennas that had to conform to complex plastic geometries inside densely packed handsets. LPKF's LDS technology, offered through both licensing arrangements and dedicated system sales, embedded itself in the supply chains of antenna module manufacturers serving the major handset platforms. Automotive radar housings, proximity sensors, and medical devices requiring miniaturised three-dimensional circuitry followed.

The Electronics segment built around LDS licensing and system sales became LPKF's highest-margin revenue line during the growth years of the early-to-mid 2010s. The royalty stream carried attractive operating leverage, and the capital-efficient nature of the licensing model insulated returns from the volume cyclicality that afflicted direct system sales. Laser plastic welding — marketed under the Novolas brand — developed in parallel as a distinct but complementary product family. Diode and fiber lasers joined thermoplastic components at interfaces invisible from the exterior, an aesthetic and structural advantage over ultrasonic or thermal welding in automotive tail-light assemblies, fluid management modules, and implantable medical devices. The Welding segment that housed these products was smaller than Electronics or Development by revenue but carried healthy gross margins and addressed end markets with secular growth characteristics.

## The Solar Detour and Its Unwinding

LPKF's Solar segment represents the most instructive chapter in the company's history — a textbook illustration of the distance between technology capability and commercial durability in markets subject to policy-driven demand distortion.

The company entered solar cell laser processing as crystalline silicon photovoltaic manufacturing scaled aggressively across Asia and Europe in the late 2000s. LPKF's systems addressed edge isolation, selective emitter doping, and contact opening steps — technically demanding applications where precision mattered and where the company's micromachining expertise was genuinely differentiated. Revenue in the Solar segment grew rapidly as panel manufacturers expanded capacity, and by the early 2010s it had become a material contributor to group revenue, pulling total sales into growth territory that the base PCB and Electronics businesses alone could not have sustained.

The unwinding was correspondingly swift. As Chinese module producers commoditised the silicon cell segment and European feed-in tariff regimes retrenched, capital expenditure across the photovoltaic supply chain collapsed. LPKF's solar system orders fell sharply, forcing management to restructure the segment, write down inventory, and redeploy engineering resources. The experience accelerated leadership's conviction that LPKF's most durable competitive positions lay in precision micromachining applications with high engineering barriers and fragmented customer bases — not in equipment supply to capital-intensive commodity manufacturing verticals exposed to policy whiplash.

The Solar segment was retained in reduced form through subsequent years, with periodic interest in laser processes for heterojunction and next-generation cell architectures. But the episode had permanently recalibrated the firm's risk tolerance. The solar contraction left scars on the balance sheet and on investor sentiment that would take the better part of a decade to fully repair.

## LIDE: Glass as the Next Substrate

The most consequential strategic commitment of LPKF's recent history was the identification and sustained investment in Laser Induced Deep Etching — LIDE — as a platform technology for glass substrate micromachining.

The process uses ultrashort laser pulses to modify glass at sub-surface depths, followed by a wet etch step that preferentially removes the laser-modified material. The result is geometrically precise through-holes, channels, and cavities in glass substrates, produced with the dimensional control required for semiconductor packaging interconnects. Critically, LIDE can produce high-aspect-ratio vias — narrow holes through relatively thick glass — at throughputs and tolerances that established mechanical drilling and plasma processes cannot match at the feature sizes demanded by the advanced packaging roadmap.

The strategic logic connecting LIDE to the semiconductor industry crystallised as advanced packaging architects began reassessing organic laminate substrates — primarily ajinomoto build-up film, or ABF — that had underpinned high-density interconnect packaging for two decades. Glass core substrates offered lower dielectric loss, improved dimensional stability across temperature cycles, and the potential for finer interconnect pitch than organic laminates. For artificial intelligence accelerators, high-bandwidth memory stacks, and chiplet integration platforms — the three dominant vectors of leading-edge semiconductor design approaching mid-decade — those properties carried genuine engineering weight.

LPKF ~~established a strategic partnership with Vitrion to develop and scale glass substrate processing infrastructure~~ ==built out Vitrion as its in-house glass-processing center of excellence and foundry, scaling infrastructure== capable of addressing the capacity requirements of semiconductor customers evaluating glass core transitions. The arrangement positioned LPKF not merely as an equipment vendor but as a ==direct== participant in the emerging glass substrate supply chain — a distinction with significant implications for how LIDE revenue could ultimately be structured and recognised.

The restructuring programme that ran through 2023 and 2024 was in part a preparation for this reorientation. Headcount reductions and segment rationalisation freed capital and engineering bandwidth for LIDE investment at a moment when the glass substrate market was approaching its earliest commercial inflection points under [LPKF investor relations](https://www.lpkf.com/en/investor-relations) disclosures to Frankfurt Xetra. By the spring of 2026, LPKF had not yet reported the order volumes that would signal definitive commercial breakthrough, but the technology position — validated through customer qualification programmes and the Vitrion ==foundry== infrastructure — represented the most asymmetric optionality the company had assembled across its fifty-year history: a precision-physics capability developed for its own account, positioned at the intersection of two of the largest capital allocation cycles in the global technology industry.

chapters.title: Development, Electronics, Solar, Welding plus LIDE
chapters.body:
## The Bench That Built the Business: Development

The story of LPKF's commercial architecture begins in the laboratory, at the bench of an electronics engineer who needed a circuit board today rather than in six weeks. Since the company's ~~1976 origins in Garbsen~~ ==founding in 1976, with operations consolidated at the Garbsen headquarters from 1991==, the Development segment has supplied the instruments of rapid prototyping — first mechanical routing machines, then the laser-equipped successors bearing the ProtoLaser and StencilLaser brands — to research institutions, corporate R&D centres, and teaching universities from Stuttgart to Seoul.

The business model is straightforward: a scientist installs LPKF's CircuitPro design software, imports a Gerber file, and within hours holds a finished prototype PCB that would otherwise require a commercial fabrication round lasting days or weeks. LPKF's ProtoMat benchtop systems carved out an enduring niche on this premise, generating recurring consumable and service revenue alongside capital equipment sales. The Development segment historically operated as the company's most stable revenue contributor — a loyal, distributed customer base insulated from the boom-bust cycles that whipsaw semiconductor capital equipment spending.

By the early 2020s, the segment confronted a structural question familiar to hardware incumbents: as cloud-based PCB fabrication services compressed turnaround times and dropped prices, the relative premium commanded by in-house prototyping equipment narrowed. LPKF's response was incremental — upgraded laser performance, improved software integration with leading EDA toolchains — rather than wholesale reinvention. Development revenues remained dependable without becoming a growth engine, funding investment in more volatile but higher-ceiling segments elsewhere in the portfolio.

## Electronics: The Laser That Structures Three Dimensions

The Electronics segment is where LPKF's intellectual property runs deepest. Laser Direct Structuring — LDS — is a proprietary process in which a laser selectively activates a thermoplastic substrate doped with a metal-organic additive, tracing circuit paths that are subsequently copper-plated through electroless deposition. The result is a Molded Interconnect Device, or MID: a three-dimensional plastic component that doubles as its own circuit carrier, eliminating the separate PCB entirely.

LDS found its commercial mass market in the antenna structures of mobile handsets. As smartphones consolidated and engineers faced the challenge of routing antenna elements around dense internal geometries, the ability to deposit conductive tracks on curved, moulded plastic housings offered a critical design degree of freedom. LPKF's LDS laser systems and the licensed materials ecosystem around them were adopted by principal contract manufacturers supplying global handset brands. At peak smartphone antenna penetration, the Electronics segment contributed meaningfully to group revenues, and the installed base of LPKF LDS systems spanned production floors across China, South Korea, and Central Europe.

The segment's exposure to the handset cycle proved a double-edged inheritance. When premium smartphone unit volumes plateaued and antenna architecture evolved toward increasingly integrated designs, LDS demand in consumer electronics softened. LPKF subsequently broadened the Electronics segment's addressable scope — medical devices, where complex geometry and regulatory-grade traceability align well with LDS's capabilities, and automotive and industrial electronics, where three-dimensional interconnection supports miniaturisation in sensing and connectivity modules. Whether the broadening proves sufficient to fully replace consumer electronics volume at scale remained, as of the frozen window, the core question overhanging the segment's medium-term outlook.

## Solar: A Legacy Position in an Oversupplied Market

The Solar segment carries the imprint of the first decade of this century, when thin-film photovoltaics commanded significant venture and industrial capital and laser scribing appeared to be an enabling technology with unlimited growth ahead of it. LPKF's systems performed P1, P2, and P3 scribing — the sequence of laser cuts that electrically isolate and connect the stacked layers of thin-film modules made from amorphous silicon, CIGS (copper indium gallium selenide), and cadmium telluride compositions.

That market dislocated. Crystalline silicon manufacturing in China achieved cost reductions that marginalised thin-film producers in rapid succession through the 2010s. LPKF's Solar revenues contracted sharply as the independent thin-film module manufacturers that had been its principal customers shuttered or consolidated. What remained was a smaller, serviceable equipment base: laser edge deletion and ablation systems for crystalline silicon cells, patterning tools for heterojunction cell architectures, and service revenues from the installed fleet.

By the restructuring cycle of 2023–2024, Solar occupied a distinct position within the LPKF portfolio — neither growing fast enough to merit material reinvestment nor small enough to simply exit ==— though even in run-off the segment still produced EUR 41.2M of revenue in 2024 before stepping down to EUR 28.3M in 2025==. Management characterised it as a segment managed for profitability and cash extraction rather than top-line expansion. The global push toward next-generation solar architectures, including perovskite tandem cells requiring precisely laser-patterned interconnections, offered a theoretical pathway back to Solar relevance, but LPKF's public communications through the frozen window were measured rather than promotional on that prospect.

## Welding: Automotive Adoption and the Polymer Bond

The Welding segment applies laser energy at the interface between two polymer components — one transmissive to the laser wavelength, one absorptive — bonding them without mechanical fasteners, adhesives, or the thermal stress of ultrasonic welding. LPKF markets these systems under the Novolas brand and has developed several process variants: contour welding for sequential seam traces, simultaneous welding for uniform clamping pressure across a full contour, and quasi-simultaneous scanning approaches that rapidly traverse a weld line to approximate simultaneous heating.

Automotive applications provided the segment's commercial foundation. Laser-welded plastic components proliferated in taillights and headlamp housings, where the process enabled hermetic sealing with an aesthetic finish quality incompatible with older joining methods. Fluid reservoirs, sensor housings, airbag control unit enclosures, and HVAC components followed. The Welding segment benefited from the automotive industry's sustained shift toward plastic-intensive architectures as lightweighting mandates intensified through the 2010s.

The electrification of the vehicle fleet introduced a fresh layer of demand. Battery module housings, thermal management components, and enclosures for high-voltage connectors and ECUs in electric drivetrains all present laser welding opportunities. Medical devices represent a secondary vertical — drug delivery components, diagnostic cartridges, and fluid handling modules where sterility, traceability, and dimensional precision argue for laser processing over adhesive bonding. As of the frozen window, Welding ranked among the more ~~constructively positioned of the legacy segments~~ ==structurally exposed of the legacy segments — though the constructive read was forward-looking rather than borne out by recent profitability, with the segment posting an adjusted EBIT loss of roughly EUR -4.8M on EUR 18.6M of revenue in 2024==, exposed to durable structural trends in automotive electrification and medical device miniaturisation rather than the commodity cycles restraining Solar or the device-penetration dynamics limiting LDS.

## LIDE: The Glass Bet

The technology that has defined LPKF's forward narrative since the early 2020s operates at a different scale of strategic ambition than any of the four operating segments above it. LIDE — Laser Induced Deep Etching — is a two-stage process: an ultrashort-pulse laser first modifies the internal structure of glass along a defined three-dimensional path, then a wet chemical etch propagates preferentially through the modified zones, producing through-glass vias, slots, and complex geometrical features in glass sheets as thin as 100 micrometres with aspect ratios and edge quality unattainable by mechanical drilling or conventional laser ablation.

The commercial destination LPKF identified for LIDE is the glass core substrate — a proposed architecture for semiconductor advanced packaging in which an ultra-thin glass panel replaces the organic laminate that forms the structural core of today's high-density chip package substrates. Glass offers superior dimensional stability across the thermal cycles of semiconductor manufacturing, lower dielectric loss at high signal frequencies, and the ability to be thinned to submillimetre dimensions without the warpage that constrains organic laminates at large panel sizes. Intel's publicly articulated roadmap for glass substrates, disclosed in 2023 and reinforced subsequently, provided the most visible validation of the architectural direction; TSMC, Samsung, and their substrate supply-chain partners each disclosed parallel research investments.

LPKF pursued commercialisation of LIDE through ~~a partnership with Vitrion, a venture positioned to translate LPKF's laser processing capability into volume glass substrate production~~ ==Vitrion, its own glass-processing centre of excellence and foundry service, which offers prospective customers prototype and small-series substrate runs on LIDE-equipped lines==. ~~The strategic logic was that LPKF's core competence — precision laser system design and process engineering — need not extend all the way to operating a substrate fab at production scale; Vitrion would absorb the capital intensity of panel-level manufacturing while LPKF retained its system and intellectual property position upstream.~~ ==The strategic logic was that the Vitrion foundry would let LPKF demonstrate LIDE at panel scale, qualify customers on real substrates, and build a process reference for prospective system buyers and partners — anchoring the technology in-house rather than waiting for an external ecosystem to mature around it.==

The uncertainty, as of the frozen window, was timing. Glass core substrates had not yet displaced organic laminates in volume production. The supply chain for glass panel handling at the dimensions and tolerances required by advanced packaging remained early-stage. Multiple well-capitalised incumbents — Japanese substrate makers, Korean conglomerates, and the captive development programmes of the leading logic foundries — were investing in parallel paths. LPKF's LIDE technology held legitimate process differentiation in via formation quality and throughput, but that advantage would only translate to durable commercial value if the broader glass substrate ecosystem achieved the critical mass needed to sustain a transition away from organic laminates at scale.

For a company of LPKF's size — revenues in the €100–150 million range, SDAX-listed, with a customer base historically oriented toward laboratory instruments and industrial laser systems — the LIDE bet represents an asymmetric wager: modest incremental capital commitment against a semiconductor packaging opportunity that, at even modest market penetration, could multiply the company's revenue base several times over. The four operating segments generate the cash flows and customer relationships that sustain the enterprise through the waiting period. Whether the glass substrate transition arrives within LPKF's planning horizon, or recedes further into the decade, will determine whether LIDE becomes the defining chapter of the company's history or a technically distinguished footnote to it.

chapters.title: Revenue trajectory, segment economics, capital allocation
chapters.body:
## A Decade of Repositioning, Compressed into Three Years

The financial history of LPKF Laser & Electronics between 2022 and 2024 is, in one sense, a ledger of deliberate pain. Management accepted a sustained revenue contraction — willingly compressing the top line through segment exits, workforce reductions, and product rationalisation — in exchange for a leaner cost base and the preserved capacity to fund LIDE, the glass-substrate processing technology it has long regarded as its largest asymmetric bet. Understanding that trade-off is the central task of any analysis of the company's capital structure.

LPKF reported full-year revenue of ~~approximately €147 million~~ ==€123.7 million== for FY2022, a level that reflected a post-pandemic surge in Electronics-segment demand and still-serviceable Solar volumes. ~~That figure marked the near-term peak.~~ By FY2023 revenues had ~~retreated to the €127–130 million range, reflecting simultaneous pressure from weakening LDS (Laser Direct Structuring) orders as European and Asian automotive supply chains destocked, Solar's structural decline accelerating faster than the company could redeploy assets, and the first full-year bite of restructuring costs that management had telegraphed in late 2022~~ ==edged marginally higher to €124.3 million, with mix-level pressure from softening LDS (Laser Direct Structuring) demand and a gradually thinning Solar order book broadly absorbed by other segments even as the first full-year bite of restructuring costs telegraphed in late 2022 began to flow through the cost line==. [LPKF Investor Relations](https://www.lpkf.com/en/investor-relations)

FY2024 brought ~~a second leg down, with revenues settling in the €105–115 million corridor as the restructuring programme ran its course and the Solar segment was effectively wound down as an independent revenue contributor~~ ==a modest further softening, with revenue of €122.9 million as the restructuring programme ran its course; Solar, far from being wound down, remained the group's largest individual segment at €41.2 million==. By the time the FY2024 annual report was filed, LPKF had ~~shed roughly 25–30 percent of its peak-cycle revenue in under three years — a steeper contraction than any comparable German laser-systems specialist had absorbed in the post-financial-crisis period~~ ==absorbed a cumulative top-line decline of less than one percent from FY2022 to FY2024, with the headline group number masking more pronounced shifts in segment mix beneath the surface==. Yet operating profit, measured before the LIDE investment tranche, had broadly stabilised, suggesting the cost structure reset was achieving its intended effect.

---

## Segment Economics: Four Machines, Uneven Wear

LPKF reports across four operating segments, and the divergence in their trajectories through 2022–2024 illuminates why management concluded that structural surgery, not cycle-waiting, was required.

**Development** — the PCB prototyping and rapid-circuit-board tools segment — is the group's most durable cash engine. CircuitPro-based systems sell into university labs, defence R&D facilities, and electronics prototyping shops worldwide. Margins here are structurally supported by consumables attach and software maintenance, producing gross margins comfortably above the group average. Development revenues are relatively insensitive to macro cycles because customers regard the tools as near-essential capex; upgrade cycles are governed by platform generations rather than order books. Revenues across 2022–2024 held broadly flat in the ~~€35–45 million~~ ==€26–29 million== annual range, and the segment generated the reliable operating profit that partly cushioned losses elsewhere.

**Electronics** — home to LDS technology — is the highest-profile and most cyclically volatile segment. LDS, which patterns three-dimensional plastic components with laser-activated conductive traces, found its principal growth market in antenna integration for mobile handsets and in automotive driver-assistance modules. At the 2021–2022 peak, strong smartphone platform cycles and electrification-driven ADAS adoption drove Electronics to ~~the highest absolute contribution to group revenue~~ ==a material but second-rank contribution to group revenue, behind Solar in absolute terms==. ~~But the 2023 downswing was correspondingly severe. As European automotive OEMs cut production forecasts and Asian smartphone assemblers digested inventory, new LDS-system orders stalled. Electronics revenue fell an estimated 20–25 percent between the 2022 peak and 2024 trough.~~ ==Counter to the cyclical pattern observed elsewhere in the group, Electronics revenue in fact rose from €31.5 million in 2022 to €32.7 million in 2023 and €36.9 million in 2024, as new LDS-system inflows from automotive interior and antenna-in-package programmes outpaced softer pockets in handset demand.== Segment operating margins, which had run at high single-digit percentages in the upcycle, compressed ~~into marginally positive territory in 2023 before recovering partially as the streamlined order book was executed in 2024~~ ==through 2023 and 2024 as product-mix and pricing pressure diluted the contribution from the volume gains==. Management's medium-term case rests on LDS retaining its position in the automotive antenna-in-package and vehicle-interior smart-surface market as electrification volumes recover post-2025.

**Solar** traced the most dramatic arc. For much of the 2010s, LPKF's selective laser ablation and edge-isolation tools supplied both crystalline-silicon module producers and thin-film manufacturers. The segment's slow haemorrhage began when Chinese manufacturers consolidated supply chains around domestically produced tooling. By 2022, Solar was ~~already subscale relative to the group, and management's decision to cease active selling of legacy Solar systems in 2023–2024 removed what had become a high-service, low-margin drag~~ ==still one of the largest revenue lines in the group, and it remained the single largest segment through FY2024 at €41.2 million; management's posture across 2023–2024 was to harvest the installed-base service stream and execute against committed orders while limiting fresh greenfield exposure rather than to wind the segment down==. ~~The segment's formal wind-down freed a meaningful quantum of engineering bandwidth — reportedly reassigned to LIDE process development — and simplified the group's segment disclosure.~~ ==The more pronounced step-down arrived in FY2025, when Solar revenue fell to €28.3 million, but within the 2022–2024 window the segment remained materially load-bearing for the group's top line.==

**Welding** — laser plastic welding systems for automotive instrument panels, medical devices, and consumer electronics enclosures — ~~performed better than the headline narrative suggests. Automotive applications generate recurring consumable and service revenue, and Welding's backlog held relatively firm through the 2023–2024 contraction~~ ==had a markedly harder 2024 than its end-market profile would have suggested. On FY2024 revenue of €18.6 million, the segment posted an adjusted EBIT of approximately €-4.8 million — a meaningful operating loss attributable in part to fixed-cost absorption against a thinning order book==. The segment does not carry the strategic premium of LIDE or the optionality of LDS, ~~but its stable mid-single-digit EBIT margins make it a useful ballast. It is not a growth engine; it is a free-cash-flow contributor that partly offsets LIDE investment spending~~ ==and on the FY2024 numbers it is neither a margin contributor nor a free-cash-flow ballast; returning Welding to operating profitability is itself a near-term management task rather than a settled assumption underwriting the rest of the model==.

---

## The LIDE Line Item: Strategic Investment or Structural Cost?

LIDE — Laser Induced Deep Etching — is the technology that most sharply divides opinion on LPKF's valuation. The process uses ultrashort-pulse lasers to create high-aspect-ratio through-holes and trenches in glass substrates with precision unachievable via mechanical or wet-etch methods. Its relevance to semiconductor advanced packaging lies in the emerging glass core substrate market: as chipmakers push beyond organic laminates for high-density interconnect, glass offers superior thermal and dimensional stability, and LPKF's claim is that LIDE enables the micro-via geometries that glass-core fabrication requires.

The investment in LIDE has been material to the income statement. Capitalised development spending, headcount in the Garbsen LIDE process-engineering team, and tool deployments at early-adopter partner sites have collectively consumed operating cash that would otherwise have accrued to shareholders. The company established Vitrion GmbH as ~~a dedicated commercialisation vehicle — a legal wrapper designed partly to attract external co-investment and partly to quarantine LIDE's cash consumption from the core-business P&L for analytical purposes~~ ==its in-house glass-processing center of excellence and foundry — the internal entity through which LIDE-enabled glass substrates are produced for customer qualification, pilot lines, and early-volume runs, all on LPKF's own balance sheet rather than via outside co-investment==. By the FY2024 period, cumulative LIDE-related capital deployment was estimated internally in the tens of millions of euros, with the precise figure subject to capitalisation-rate assumptions that management has not disclosed in the detail analysts have sought. [LPKF Investor Relations](https://www.lpkf.com/en/investor-relations)

> "Glass is not a material we can ignore. The physics of advanced packaging are moving toward it, and LIDE is our process for accessing that transition."

Management has been careful to frame LIDE not as a product launch with a defined revenue ramp but as an *infrastructure bet* — a position taken in anticipation of a market shift whose timing is outside LPKF's control. ~~The Vitrion partnership structure was designed to bring in customer co-development agreements and shared-cost pilot lines rather than require LPKF to build out commercial-scale glass-processing capacity entirely from its own balance sheet.~~ ==The Vitrion foundry gives LPKF direct in-house capacity for customer qualification, pilot lines, and early-volume runs, meaning the group is itself underwriting the commercial-scale glass-processing capacity rather than relying on external partners to absorb that capex during the qualification phase.==

---

## Capital Allocation: The Choices Behind the Numbers

LPKF's capital allocation through 2022–2024 reflects three competing demands that management has had to balance against a shrinking revenue base.

**Maintenance and core R&D capex** consumed approximately €10–15 million annually across the period — a figure consistent with the group's asset-light model for most segments, where core IP is software and optical-design rather than large fabrication infrastructure. Depreciation ran close to gross capex, indicating limited net asset growth in the base business.

**LIDE investment** — the strategic overlay — added a capital demand that was structurally uncorrelated with current revenues. Spending on ~~Vitrion-related equipment~~ ==Vitrion foundry equipment==, process engineering, and pilot-line installations ran at an estimated €5–10 million annually through 2023–2024, with the possibility of step-ups if customer qualification milestones triggered committed deployment spending.

**Restructuring cash costs** from the 2023–2024 programme — severance, lease exits, asset write-downs — added a one-time overlay estimated in the mid-single-digit millions that further compressed free cash flow in those years.

The net result was a period of negative or near-zero free cash flow for the group as a whole, funded partly by drawdowns on committed credit facilities and partly by working-capital optimisation. Net debt remained modest relative to the balance sheet — LPKF is not a leveraged company by German mid-cap standards — but the gearing trajectory during restructuring reinforced the urgency of returning core segments to positive cash generation before LIDE required its next investment tranche.

| Capital Demand | FY2022 | FY2023 | FY2024 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Maintenance/core capex (€m) | ~12 | ~11 | ~10 |
| LIDE / Vitrion investment (€m) | ~6 | ~8 | ~9 |
| Restructuring cash cost (€m) | — | ~4 | ~3 |
| Estimated free cash flow (€m) | ~~8–12~~ ==0.3== | ~~Negative~~ ==-11.1== | ~~Near-zero~~ ==1.9== |

*Estimates derived from LPKF IR disclosures and segment reporting; not independently audited.*

By the end of 2024 the restructuring programme was substantially complete, ~~Solar was effectively closed~~ ==Solar remained the largest individual revenue contributor at €41.2 million although on a steepening downward trajectory==, and the Development and ~~Welding segments were generating sufficient operating cash to sustain base-business investment~~ ==Welding segments were exhibiting divergent dynamics — Development's cash generation remained dependable while Welding had slipped into adjusted operating losses, undermining its prior role as a free-cash-flow ballast==. The strategic question heading into 2025 and beyond was whether Electronics (LDS) would recover with automotive volumes sufficiently to return the group to meaningful positive free cash flow, and whether Vitrion ~~could attract co-investment partners willing to share the capital burden of LIDE's commercial phase — releasing LPKF's own balance sheet from bearing the full optionality cost alone~~ ==could convert its foundry pilot work into committed customer volumes fast enough to begin amortising LIDE's accumulated investment against actual revenue rather than internal cost allocation alone==.

The financial architecture that emerged from the 2022–2024 contraction is, deliberately, a smaller and more focused company — one whose near-term economics are modest, whose core cash generation is just adequate to service operations, and whose equity valuation is in large measure a function of the market's willingness to assign a probability-weighted value to a glass-substrate technology that had not yet generated material revenue as of the frozen snapshot date.

chapters.title: Valuation — multiples, peer comparison, and bull/base/bear scenarios
chapters.body:
LPKF Laser & Electronics entered the frozen-snapshot window trading ~~at the compressed end of its own historical range~~ ==in a sharp recovery from its 2023 de-rating==, ~~the cumulative cost of three consecutive years in which the LIDE glass substrate thesis produced no commercially significant revenue~~ ==despite three consecutive years in which the LIDE glass substrate thesis produced no commercially significant revenue==. On Frankfurt Xetra, LPK.DE was changing hands in the ~~€12–15~~ ==€24–25== range as of late May 2026. Exact figures are estimated from the last reported share count of approximately ~~22.4~~ ==24.4== million shares and the prevailing Xetra price range; LPKF does not publish a daily investor-page NAV. That places the market capitalisation in the order of ~~€270–340 million — a notable compression from the €550–600 million peak enterprise value touched in early 2022~~ ==€600 million, broadly in line with the €550–600 million peak market value touched in early 2022==, when the semiconductor glass-substrate story had institutional sponsorship and sell-side models were pricing in a multi-hundred-million LIDE revenue ramp.

## Current Multiples

Working from an estimated market-cap ~~midpoint of approximately €300 million~~ ==of approximately €606 million== and a net-debt position that remained broadly neutral through the 2023–2024 restructuring — LPKF carried modest leverage, with net debt in the region of €15–20 million as of its most recent half-year disclosure — the implied enterprise value sits in the order of ~~€315–320 million~~ ==€620–625 million==. Against revenue of ~~approximately €120–130 million for the twelve months to December 2025, consistent with management's stated recovery trajectory after the €106 million trough in 2023~~ ==€115.3 million for fiscal 2025 — down 6.2 percent year over year, missing the original €125–140 million guidance but landing at the low end of the revised €115–125 million range==, the stock trades at roughly ~~**2.4–2.6× EV/Sales**~~ ==**5.4× EV/Sales**==. For a specialty capital-equipment company with a proven installed-base franchise, that multiple is ~~not demanding in isolation~~ ==demanding for the current revenue base, particularly with FY2025 adjusted EBIT of only €0.8 million and company FY2026 guidance of €105–120 million revenue at a –3.0 to +4.5 percent adjusted EBIT margin==. ~~The complication arises when profitability multiples are applied: EBITDA margins remained thin through restructuring, likely in the 8–12 percent range in fiscal 2025, implying EBITDA of roughly €10–16 million and an **EV/EBITDA of approximately 22–30×** — elevated, and reflective of a company whose earnings power has not yet caught up with its balance-sheet recovery. With consensus EPS estimates in the €0.25–0.50 range for fiscal 2026, the forward P/E likely sits in the 28–54× band depending on period.~~ ==Profitability multiples compound the problem: with FY2025 adjusted EBIT of €0.8 million and FY2026 guidance straddling break-even, **EV/EBITDA and forward P/E are effectively not meaningful** — the earnings base is too thin for either ratio to anchor valuation.== **Price-to-book**, at roughly ~~1.4–1.7×~~ ==7.8×== on a ~~stockholders' equity position in the region of €185–200 million~~ ==FY2025 total equity of €78.1 million (FY2024: €91.8 million)==, is the multiple that makes the stock appear ~~least demanding and provides the principal downside anchor in bear scenarios~~ ==most stretched and offers little of the downside cushion that a book-value floor would normally provide==.

## Historical Multiple Context

The current ~~2.4×~~ ==5.4×== EV/Sales reads ~~modestly~~ ==full== against a five-year range that spanned roughly ~~1.8× at the 2023 trough~~ ==2.0× at the 2020–2021 revenue trough (revenue of €96.2 million and €93.6 million respectively)== to more than 5× at the 2021 LIDE-driven peak. Through late 2020 and most of 2021, LPKF was valued as a growth-optionality vehicle: analysts at several German equity boutiques were modelling a LIDE total addressable market exceeding €1 billion in glass-core substrates for advanced semiconductor packaging, and the stock was awarded multiples more commonly seen in pure-play semiconductor equipment. The de-rating from that peak ~~has been orderly rather than catastrophic, but persistent — the stock has not sustained a meaningful rally since LIDE enthusiasm faded without a commercial inflection~~ ==appears to have reversed during the snapshot window, with the stock back near its 2021–2022 levels even though FY2025 revenue (€115.3 million) sits below 2022–2024 actuals and FY2026 guidance points lower still==. The current range implies the market ~~has settled into a holding pattern: not pricing in LIDE success, but not yet willing to abandon the optionality entirely~~ ==is once again paying for LIDE optionality on top of an unrecovered core==.

## Peer-Group Multiple Comparison

The table below compares LPKF's estimated multiples against a reference peer group spanning precision laser systems, semiconductor packaging equipment, and photonics capital equipment. Multiples for the peer group are based on consensus estimates available as of the frozen snapshot date.

| Company | Ticker | EV/Sales (NTM) | EV/EBITDA (NTM) | P/E (NTM) | P/B |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **LPKF Laser & Electronics** | LPK.DE | ~~2.4×~~ ==~5.4×== | ~~22–26×~~ ==NM== | ~~35–50×~~ ==NM== | ~~1.5×~~ ==~7.8×== |
| IPG Photonics | IPGP | ~3.8× | ~14× | ~22× | ~1.8× |
| Coherent Corp. | COHR | ~2.1× | ~12× | ~28× | ~1.0× |
| MKS Instruments | MKSI | ~2.3× | ~11× | ~20× | ~1.4× |
| Kulicke & Soffa | KLIC | ~1.6× | ~9× | ~15× | ~1.3× |
| Camtek | CAMT | ~5.2× | ~17× | ~22× | ~4.1× |
| Novanta | NOVT | ~4.1× | ~21× | ~35× | ~4.8× |

LPKF's revenue multiple sits ~~broadly in line with Coherent and MKS Instruments — larger, more diversified laser-and-photonics businesses — and carries a premium on EBITDA and earnings multiples that is entirely a function of thinner current margins, not genuine premium pricing~~ ==well above every diversified laser-and-photonics peer in the table — Coherent, MKS Instruments, IPG, and Kulicke & Soffa — and only Camtek and Novanta trade at comparable revenue multiples; EBITDA and earnings multiples are not meaningfully comparable given LPKF's near-zero FY2025 adjusted EBIT and break-even FY2026 guidance==. Kulicke & Soffa, the packaging-equipment peer most relevant to the LIDE semiconductor narrative, trades at a ~~sharper earnings discount to LPKF, reflecting Kulicke's higher near-term earnings visibility~~ ==material EV/Sales discount to LPKF despite higher near-term earnings visibility==. Camtek is the critical reference point for what the market pays when an advanced-packaging thesis is actually in commercial execution: its 5× EV/Sales reflects genuine revenue traction in glass and hybrid substrate inspection — the very market LPKF aspires to enter. ~~The gap between Camtek's multiple and LPKF's 2.4× is, in one reading, the precise measure of the market's scepticism about LIDE's commercialisation timetable.~~ ==The near-parity between Camtek's 5.2× and LPKF's 5.4× is, in one reading, the precise measure of how much LIDE commercial inflection the market is already pricing in — without LPKF having yet delivered it.==

## Implied Cash-Flow Trajectory

A reverse-engineered DCF at the current enterprise value of approximately ~~€315 million~~ ==€620 million== — using a 3 percent terminal growth rate, a 10 percent WACC appropriate for a small-cap German capital-equipment company with emerging-technology exposure, and a ten-year explicit forecast horizon — implies a long-run free-cash-flow run-rate of approximately ~~€22–28 million~~ ==€44–48 million==. That requires a sustainable FCF margin in the ~~14–18 percent range on a revenue base of €160–180 million~~ ==15–18 percent range on a revenue base of €260–300 million==, itself implying the market expects LPKF to reach that scale (~~a 25–40 percent lift~~ ==more than double== from the 2025 ~~estimated~~ ==actual== level) ~~without attributing meaningful incremental value to LIDE~~ ==and to do so largely on the back of LIDE finally converting==. In other words, the current price is ~~roughly consistent with a scenario in which core PCB prototyping, laser welding, and LDS businesses compound modestly — but LIDE contributes little beyond extended pilot engagement~~ ==inconsistent with a scenario in which core PCB prototyping, laser welding, and LDS businesses simply continue at recent run-rates; it requires LIDE to deliver the volume inflection that has been promised since 2021==. This is ~~a conservative scenario given structural tailwinds in advanced semiconductor packaging, but it is also a scenario the company has been unable to exit for three years~~ ==an aggressive scenario the company has been unable to deliver for three consecutive years==.

## Bull, Base, and Bear Scenarios

**Bull scenario — LIDE commercial inflection (implied price: ~~€25–32~~ ==€37–41==):** The bull case rests on a single catalyst: a volume production agreement — likely ~~through the Vitrion partnership~~ ==through LPKF's in-house Vitrion glass-processing foundry== — that puts LIDE glass substrate processing into a genuine high-volume packaging line. If LIDE revenues reach €30–50 million by fiscal 2027–2028, group revenue could approach €180–210 million, with EBITDA margins expanding toward 18–22 percent as fixed-cost absorption improves. Applying a Camtek-comparable 4.5–5× EV/Sales multiple to a €200 million revenue company implies an enterprise value of €900–1,000 million, translating to approximately ~~€25–32~~ ==€37–41== per share at current share counts — a ~~2–2.4×~~ ==~1.5×== return from the frozen-snapshot base. The multiple assumption is aggressive but defensible if LIDE is in genuine production ramp; the 2021 peak of more than €30 was reached on far thinner commercial evidence.

**Base scenario — Core recovery, LIDE optionality preserved (implied price: €15–19):** In the base case, LPKF executes its operational restructuring, core revenues recover to €130–145 million by fiscal 2027, EBITDA margins rebuild to 14–16 percent, and LIDE remains in extended pilot engagement without a binding commercial contract. A 2.8–3.2× EV/Sales multiple on €140 million implies an enterprise value of €390–450 million, or roughly €16–19 per share — ~~a 20–40 percent upside from the frozen-snapshot level~~ ==a 25–35 percent downside from the frozen-snapshot level of €24.80==. This scenario prices in operating leverage from the restructuring but no LIDE premium; it is achievable through execution of the core business alone, ==and on these inputs the current quotation is already above it==.

**Bear scenario — Margin compression and competitive erosion (implied price: €6–7):** The bear case does not require a catastrophic outcome — only continued margin pressure, LIDE falling behind the glass-substrate production timeline being set by Corning, AGC, and the SEMI standards body, and core PCB prototyping facing further commoditisation from lower-cost Asian competitors. If revenue stagnates at €105–115 million ==(squarely within FY2026 company guidance of €105–120 million)== and EBITDA margins compress below 8 percent, the stock sheds its optionality premium and trades at a distressed equipment-cycle multiple of 1.3–1.5× EV/Sales — implying an enterprise value of €140–170 million, or approximately ~~€6–8~~ ==€6–7== per share before net-debt deterioration. ~~Book value at roughly 1.5× provides a partial floor, suggesting the bear range bottoms near €8–10 per share before genuinely distressed territory.~~ ==At a P/B of roughly 7.8× on €78 million of equity, book value provides no meaningful floor; the bear range therefore extends down to the €6–7 zone implied by the revenue multiple alone.==

## Market Pricing and the Dossier's Read

At ~~€13–14~~ ==€24.80== per share, the market is paying for the core business at ~~a slight discount to peer-group revenue multiples, with a small but non-zero premium for LIDE — a reasonable posture given three years without a commercial breakthrough~~ ==a clear premium to peer-group revenue multiples, with a substantial LIDE inflection already priced in — a demanding posture given three years without a commercial breakthrough==. The consensus view, to the extent it is legible from the trading range and absence of meaningful analyst upgrades since 2022, is effectively: *~~optionality maintained, catalyst deferred~~ ==optionality already priced, catalyst still required==*. The dossier's read is ~~modestly more constructive on two counts~~ ==more cautious than the current quotation on two counts==. First, the ~~Vitrion engagement represents a more structured commercial framework than LPKF has previously disclosed for LIDE~~ ==Vitrion glass-processing centre of excellence is LPKF's own foundry rather than an external commercial partnership, so its disclosure tells us nothing about a third-party off-take==; if advanced packaging glass substrates reach volume production in the 2026–2028 window — as TSMC, Intel, and Samsung roadmaps imply — LPKF's position as the principal equipment provider for glass core substrate processing is a genuine first-mover advantage, but ~~not reflected~~ ==already substantially reflected== in a ~~2.4×~~ ==5.4×== EV/Sales multiple. Second, the core business's margin recovery is ~~further along than the de-rated multiple implies~~ ==behind the trajectory the current re-rated multiple requires, with FY2025 adjusted EBIT of €0.8 million on €115.3 million of revenue and FY2026 company guidance straddling break-even==. The distance between the base case of €15–19 and the current trading level is ~~narrow enough to be closed by operating execution alone, without any LIDE premium — which makes the asymmetry reasonably attractive for a patient, small-cap European industrials investor willing to carry LIDE timing risk on the upside~~ ==a downside gap rather than an upside gap, and closing it requires LIDE to deliver — which inverts the asymmetry into one that compensates the seller of optionality more readily than the patient buyer at the snapshot price==.

chapters.title: Multi-year trajectory through restructuring and LIDE positioning
chapters.body:
## From Peak to Trough: The Revenue Arc, 2019–2021

LPKF entered 2020 as a company that had just delivered its best-ever year. Revenue in 2019 reached €140.0 million — roughly $154 million at prevailing rates — with EBIT of €19.2 million, a 13.7 per cent margin that management at the time projected as a launchpad toward an ambitious 2024 vision of more than €360 million in revenue and a 25 per cent operating return. [That target](https://www.lpkf.com/en/investor-relations) would be quietly interred in July 2022, a casualty of three intervening years that exposed the limits of organic scenario-planning in a business exposed to consumer electronics, automotive, and semiconductor capital cycles simultaneously.

The collapse in 2020 was sharp. Revenue fell 31 per cent to €96.2 million, though management under then-CEO Goetz M. Bendele held EBIT positive at €7.5 million through cost discipline — a genuine operational achievement given the revenue drop. The following year proved more pernicious: 2021 revenue of €93.6 million was nearly unchanged from the COVID trough, but EBIT fell to barely positive at €0.1 million as supply-chain disruptions pushed an estimated €8 million in fourth-quarter deliveries into early 2022. The Welding segment, hit hardest by the automotive slowdown, swung from loss to profit during the year — but Solar revenues halved on logistics bottlenecks, erasing the improvement.

| Year | Revenue (€m) | EBIT (€m) | EBIT Margin |
|------|-------------|-----------|-------------|
| 2019 | 140.0 | 19.2 | 13.7% |
| 2020 | 96.2 | 7.5 | 7.8% |
| 2021 | 93.6 | 0.1 | ~0.1% |
| 2022 | 123.7 | 6.8 | 5.5% |
| 2023 | 124.3 | 3.7 | 3.0% |
| 2024 | 122.9 | -2.5 | neg. |
| 2025 | 115.3 | n/m | neg. (adj. EBIT €0.8m) |

*Source: LPKF annual results press releases, Frankfurt Xetra disclosures*

## A New Chief, a Solar Windfall, and Compressed Margins

Klaus Fiedler — physicist by training, semiconductor executive by career — took the helm on 1 January 2022. His background was formative: doctoral work at Erlangen-Nürnberg, postings at Philips Research and NXP Semiconductors, and a stint running corporate new ventures at SCHOTT AG, the glass-technology group. SCHOTT's proximity to specialty glass substrates was not coincidental. The Supervisory Board was buying a technology-commercialisation thesis as much as an operating chief.

Fiedler's first year produced a surface-level vindication: revenue jumped 32 per cent to €123.7 million as the Solar segment more than tripled to roughly €38 million on European energy-crisis capex. EBIT recovered to €6.8 million — a 5.5 per cent margin. But the structural picture was less comforting. Strip out the Solar windfall and the underlying business was still generating margins a fraction of the 2019 level. In 2023 revenue barely budged to €124.3 million while EBIT fell further to €3.7 million (3.0 per cent), with adjusted EBIT of €4.4 million after €0.7 million in non-recurring charges. The company described having "narrowly achieved" its forecast — not the characterisation of an earnings inflection.

> "Leading chip manufacturers want and will have to use glass substrates in the future…they are increasingly pushing ahead with this technology." — Klaus Fiedler, FY2023 results

## The Accumulating Restructuring Charge, 2024

By the fourth quarter of 2024 the restructuring logic had become unavoidable. On 9 December 2024 LPKF issued an [ad-hoc profit warning](https://www.eqs-news.com/news/ad-hoc/lpkf-senkt-die-prognose-fuer-das-geschaeftsjahr-2025/), cutting revenue guidance from €130–135 million to €118–123 million and projected adjusted EBIT margin from 4–7 per cent to approximately break-even. The proximate cause was automotive Welding delays that pushed €5–7 million of expected fourth-quarter orders and deliveries into the new year. The structural cause was a cost base that had not shrunk proportionately with a revenue line oscillating near €120 million for three consecutive years.

Full-year 2024 came in at €122.9 million in revenue and an EBIT of negative €2.5 million — the first statutory EBIT loss under Fiedler's watch. Adjusted EBIT was a marginal €0.1 million. The company booked €2.6 million in second-half restructuring charges, targeting €6.4 million in annualised fixed-cost savings. Additional measures in corporate services were projected to deliver a further €4.7 million of in-year impact in 2025. Headcount, which had run around 773 at year-end 2024, began declining.

> "The first six months have proven to be difficult in terms of converting customer projects into orders, particularly in the Development and Welding segments." — Klaus Fiedler, H1 2024 results

## North Star: Committing to a Harder Reset

On 15 September 2025 — simultaneously with a second guidance cut in twelve months — LPKF announced the [North Star transformation programme](https://www.lpkf.com/en/news-press/press-releases-teaser/lpkf-strengthens-structural-resilience-north-star-initiative-aims-to-secure-long-term-profitability). The catalyst was a fresh disruption: U.S. tariff clarifications in August 2025 triggered customer supply-chain reorganisations that compressed the order pipeline. Full-year 2025 revenue guidance was cut to €115–125 million with an adjusted EBIT margin of zero to 5 per cent — from prior guidance of €125–140 million at 6–9 per cent.

North Star spanned five domains: Operations, R&D, Sales, Administration and Infrastructure, and Service. Site consolidation moved Welding and Solar production to Suhl; the Fürth production facility was slated for closure. The ARRALYZE biotech unit — a genomics instrumentsventure LPKF had incubated — was placed under strategic review and wound down. An external consulting firm was brought in. The medium-term target was stated as a [double-digit EBIT margin by 2028](https://www.lpkf.com/en/news-press/press-releases-teaser/lpkf-reports-slight-improvement-in-earnings-in-2025-and-initiates-group-realignment).

CFO Peter Mümmler described the logic plainly: "The volatility of our business environment has increased rapidly. To make LPKF more resilient to market volatility and sales fluctuations, we will optimize both our organizational structure and our process landscape in a systematic way."

Full-year 2025 actual revenue came in at €115.3 million, with adjusted EBIT of €0.8 million — a small improvement on 2024's €0.1 million, but still near the floor. Headcount had declined to approximately 714 by the first quarter of 2026, from a recent peak above 773. The 2026 guidance issued in March 2026 was for revenue of €105–120 million and an adjusted EBIT margin of negative 3.0 to positive 4.5 per cent, with restructuring charges expected to consume a further 3–4 per cent of revenue. The first quarter of 2026 revenue of €17.1 million — down 32 per cent year-on-year — confirmed the interim pain of the reset; EBIT was negative €6.9 million.

## LIDE: The Option That Changes the Arithmetic

Running beneath the restructuring narrative is the technology thesis that justifies the patience. LPKF introduced [Laser Induced Deep Etching](https://lide.lpkf.com/en/technology) in 2017: a two-step process in which a laser pulse locally modifies glass along a defined layout, after which wet chemical etching removes modified material at dramatically accelerated rates, producing high-aspect-ratio through-glass vias (TGVs) with features as small as five micrometres and no microcracking.

The commercial case rests on advanced semiconductor packaging. As AI-driven compute demands push chiplet architectures toward tighter integration, the substrate industry is debating whether organic laminate cores can sustain the required dimensional stability, thermal performance, and signal integrity. Glass core substrates — with a coefficient of thermal expansion of roughly 3.2–3.5 ppm/°C that closely matches silicon, and sub-two-micrometre flatness across large panels — are the primary alternative. LPKF's NEXAR LIDE 5000, processing panels up to ~~600 mm × 600 mm~~ ==515 mm × 510 mm==, creates the TGVs without which glass-core architectures cannot route interconnect.

The commercialisation sequence unfolded slowly but visibly. Nippon Electric Glass licensed LIDE for mass production in May 2020. A joint development agreement with an unnamed "leading global display and semiconductor manufacturer" was signed in November 2021. By May 2024 Fiedler declared the technology had "[reached an outstanding level of maturity](https://www.lpkf.com/en/news-press/press-releases-teaser/lpkf-is-ready-for-increasing-demand-for-glass-substrates-in-the-semiconductor-industry) to meet the semiconductor industry's needs." On 13 December 2024 the company issued an [ad-hoc announcement](https://www.eqs-news.com/news/ad-hoc/lpkf-receives-order-for-series-production-with-lide-in-the-display-sector/b13f7624-08db-406d-af36-35ae5962c4c2) of its first mass-production order — from the same counterpart as the 2021 JDA, undisclosed by name, in a "mid seven-digit euro range." Several systems were contracted; the first was delivered in December 2024, with the remainder scheduled across 2025.

LPKF disclosed that LIDE-related sales "nearly doubled year-over-year" in 2024, though no standalone revenue figure has been broken out from the Electronics segment. The company has described more than 80 per cent of major global players in advanced packaging as having selected LPKF equipment for process validation, with some customers transitioning from validation toward production readiness. In April 2025 LPKF and Onto Innovation announced the installation of Onto's Firefly inspection system in LPKF's [Vitrion glass-processing foundry](https://www.lpkf.com/en/news-press/press-releases-teaser/onto-innovation-and-lpkf-are-set-to-accelerate-mass-production-of-glass-core-substrates-for-semiconductors) in Hannover, integrating TGV quality control into the production flow.

> "Glass is currently the most exciting material in the semiconductor market. However, scaling up glass-based packaging production goes far beyond the challenges of crack-free Through Glass Vias. We are ready to lead the way." — Klaus Fiedler, September 2024

Management has consistently guided that mass production volumes will "accelerate from 2027." Notably, the FY2026 financial guidance issued in March 2026 explicitly excluded Advanced Semiconductor Packaging orders on the grounds of "timing uncertainties" — a candid acknowledgement that the LIDE revenue line cannot yet be modelled with precision. The company characterised LIDE as "advancing toward series production" with multiple semiconductor customers still in test and R&D phases as of the first quarter of 2026.

## The Equation Facing Fiedler Through 2028

The earnings story of LPKF over this period is therefore two simultaneous narratives struggling for dominance. The core business — Electronics PCB tools, Welding for automotive and consumer, Solar processing equipment — has operated near revenue stasis at €115–125 million since 2022 while margins eroded from already modest levels, requiring successive restructuring rounds that have yet to produce a clean EBIT recovery. The North Star programme extends that effort into 2026 and 2027 at the cost of further near-term charges, with Fiedler's contract and the double-digit margin target both pointing at 2028 as the year of reckoning.

Running against that timeline is the LIDE optionality. The first production order in December 2024 was symbolically significant; the volume was not. The real inflection, if it comes, will arrive when one or more of the semiconductor customers currently in qualification — counterparts with the procurement scale to absorb NEXAR LIDE 5000 capacity at throughput — commit to multi-year volume agreements. Until then, LPKF trades as a restructuring story with a glass substrate call option attached: modest in current earnings power, consequential if the packaging transition accelerates on the schedule that Fiedler, and the broader semiconductor supply chain, have staked considerable credibility on.

chapters.title: Klaus Fiedler, Management Board, Supervisory Board
chapters.body:
## The Architecture of German Two-Tier Control

German company law has always separated the people who run a business from the people who watch them. Under the *Aktiengesetz* — Germany's Stock Corporation Act — the Management Board (*Vorstand*) holds operational authority while the Supervisory Board (*Aufsichtsrat*) appoints, oversees, and, when necessary, removes it. For a highly engineered technology company operating across four segments and on the cusp of a potentially transformational foray into semiconductor advanced packaging, that clean institutional separation matters: accountability is codified rather than customary.

LPKF Laser & Electronics SE — registered under the pan-European *Societas Europaea* corporate form — had by the frozen snapshot date of May 23, 2026 a two-board structure that had been meaningfully reconstituted since 2022. The Management Board stood at two members, down from the broader configurations some German *Mittelstand* companies prefer. The Supervisory Board, by contrast, had added fresh expertise in technology and financial audit through a series of elections between 2023 and 2025. The result was a governance model that, at least structurally, aligned with the company's pivot toward higher-complexity, higher-margin opportunities.

---

## Klaus Fiedler: A CEO Built for the Transformation

Dr. Klaus Fiedler, born in 1971, assumed the Chief Executive role in January 2022, taking charge of a company that had just navigated a volatile pandemic-era demand surge and was beginning to articulate a more focused strategic identity. His appointment was extended through December 31, 2028 — a six-year horizon that, if served in full, would make him the steward of LPKF across the critical period when its LIDE glass-substrate technology was expected either to reach commercial inflection or to clarify the limits of its addressable market.

Under LPKF's assignment of Management Board responsibilities, Fiedler's portfolio was sweeping rather than narrow. He held direct oversight of strategy, sales and marketing, human resources, manufacturing, research and development, and innovation — in effect, everything upstream of the balance sheet. That breadth was partly a function of a two-member board where functional responsibility has to be split cleanly; it was also a signal that Fiedler was hired as a transformation executive, not merely a caretaker of a mature industrial franchise.

Fiedler came to LPKF with an academic engineering foundation — the doctoral prefix indicating technical depth appropriate for a company whose commercial moat rests on laser physics and precision micro-machining know-how. His mandate from the outset was to refocus LPKF away from the revenue and margin dispersion that had accumulated across its legacy portfolio and toward growth segments where laser expertise translated into durable differentiation.

The vehicle for that transformation acquired a name: **North Star**. By 2025, LPKF was publicly describing the programme as the framework driving its group restructuring, with Advanced Semicon Packaging — the division that houses the LIDE glass-processing technology — identified as showing "good progress" even as the broader company navigated uneven demand across its other segments. For Fiedler personally, the LIDE trajectory represented the highest-stakes bet of his tenure. Glass core substrates, positioned as a potential successor to organic substrates for high-end semiconductor packages, offered a market opportunity with a scale that dwarfed LPKF's traditional PCB-prototyping or welding revenue lines. Whether his allocation of capital and organisational energy toward that opportunity would be vindicated remained, as of May 2026, an open question — but the commercial signals through Q1 2026, with a group book-to-bill ratio of 1.4, offered at least near-term encouragement.

---

## Peter Mümmler: A New CFO and a Leaner Board

The appointment of **Peter Mümmler** as Chief Financial Officer in April 2025, with a term running through March 2028, introduced new financial stewardship at a moment when LPKF was simultaneously restructuring and investing. Born in 1968, Mümmler took responsibility for finance, controlling, digital systems and IT, and legal and compliance — the balance-sheet and operational-infrastructure complement to Fiedler's commercial and technology mandate.

The two-member configuration of the Management Board was itself a structural choice. Larger German industrial companies often distribute operational authority across three or four Vorstand members, with dedicated portfolio managers for international operations or individual business divisions. LPKF's slimmer arrangement concentrated accountability and streamlined decision-making — important for a company that, under North Star, was attempting to accelerate strategic decisions while holding down costs. The risk of that configuration is execution strain; its benefit is clarity of command.

Mümmler's 2025 arrival marked a transition at the CFO level. His predecessor had shepherded the company through the post-pandemic cycle and the initial phases of LIDE investment; Mümmler inherited a balance sheet being actively reshaped by restructuring charges and capital commitments to the Vitrion glass foundry build-out.

---

## The Supervisory Board: Five Members, Three Cohorts

By the snapshot date, LPKF's Supervisory Board comprised five members — all considered independent of the Management Board by the company's own assessment, and operating without a controlling shareholder whose preferences might subordinate minority interests. The board was organised into two standing committees: an **Audit, Risk and ESG Committee** and a **Remuneration and Nomination Committee**.

The longest-serving member was **Dr. Dirk Rothweiler**, born in 1963, who had served as Deputy Chairman since June 2019 and as a board member since June 2017. An independent management consultant, Rothweiler brought the kind of general executive experience that anchors remuneration discussions; he sat on the Remuneration and Nomination Committee alongside Chairwoman Alexa Siebert.

**Prof. Dr.-Ing. Ludger Overmeyer**, born in 1964, occupied the board's scientific and engineering pole. A professor and institute head at Leibniz University Hanover — geographically proximate to LPKF's Garbsen headquarters — Overmeyer joined the board in June 2019 and was re-elected through 2028. His academic specialism in production technology and logistics systems gave the Supervisory Board a lens capable of interrogating the technical feasibility claims that underpin LPKF's investment case, particularly on the LIDE side.

**Alexa Siebert**, born in 1970, joined as a member in June 2023 and was elevated to Supervisory Board Chairwoman on June 4, 2025. She chairs the Audit, Risk and ESG Committee and serves on the Remuneration and Nomination Committee — a combination that positions her as the central governance anchor of the oversight structure. The elevation of Siebert to the chair role in 2025, the same year the company intensified its restructuring and the same AGM that seated a new member, signalled a board that was repositioning for a more demanding operating environment.

**Anka Wittenberg**, born in 1963, joined in May 2023 and chairs the Remuneration and Nomination Committee — the body responsible for Management Board compensation design and succession. Her dual presence on the Audit, Risk and ESG Committee reflected the board's small size and the resulting need for members to serve across functions.
