The newest arrival was **Paul Owsianowski**, born in 1987, elected at the June 2025 AGM. At 37 or 38 years old at the snapshot date, Owsianowski represented the youngest perspective on the board, seated on the Audit, Risk and ESG Committee alongside Siebert and Wittenberg. His election coincided with the update to LPKF's Articles of Incorporation in June 2025, a further signal that the board's composition and governing documents were being refreshed in step with the company's strategic evolution.

---

## LIDE, Vitrion, and the Question of Segment Leadership

Below Management Board level, the LIDE glass-processing franchise operated through **Vitrion**, a dedicated division positioned as an end-to-end glass-processing foundry service under the branding *Vitrion® by LPKF®*. LPKF was the inventor of both the LIDE® laser-induced deep-etching process and the Tensor® Bonding methodology, which together formed the technological foundation of Vitrion's glass microstructuring capabilities.

The division served markets including MEMS, RF technologies, photonic systems, and — most consequentially for LPKF's long-term valuation — semiconductor advanced packaging, where glass core substrates were being positioned as a potential alternative to organic materials for high-performance compute packages. As of the snapshot date, LPKF did not publicly disclose named divisional or programme leadership for Vitrion below the Management Board level. Strategic ownership of LIDE sat with Fiedler as the CEO responsible for R&D and innovation; commercial and financial execution of the Vitrion foundry model fell within Mümmler's controlling remit.

---

## Governance Alignment with Strategic Risk

The governance architecture that Fiedler and the reconstituted Supervisory Board had assembled by mid-2026 was calibrated for a company in transition. The Management Board was small enough to move quickly; the Supervisory Board's independence, its refreshed membership, and its committee structure provided the oversight framework that LPKF's Prime Standard listing on Deutsche Börse — and its obligations under the German Corporate Governance Code — demanded.

The critical variable was whether the board's oversight mechanisms were well-matched to the asymmetric nature of the LIDE opportunity: a technology investment whose full commercial return lay beyond the normal two-to-three-year horizon of annual target-setting, requiring patient capital stewardship and an oversight body capable of distinguishing developmental setbacks from strategic failure. Overmeyer's technical profile, Siebert's audit and risk focus, and Fiedler's mandate extending through 2028 together suggested that LPKF had deliberately constructed the conditions for a long-duration technology bet — even if the market, quarter by quarter, continued to demand shorter-cycle evidence of progress.

---

*Primary sources: [LPKF Laser & Electronics SE — Management](https://www.lpkf.com/en/company/management); [LPKF Corporate Governance](https://www.lpkf.com/en/investor-relations/corporate-governance/); [Vitrion by LPKF](https://vitrion.lpkf.com/en/); [LPKF Corporate News](https://www.lpkf.com/en/investor-relations/publications/corporate-news); Frankfurt Xetra, LPK.DE.*

chapters.title: PCB prototyping customers, automotive welding, electronics, emerging LIDE
chapters.body:
## The Foundation: PCB Prototyping's Global Laboratory Network

When electronics engineers needed a circuit board built in hours rather than weeks, they turned to LPKF. The company's Development segment — anchored by the ProtoMat and ProtoLaser product families — had by the mid-2020s placed machines in an estimated several thousand laboratories, design centers, and university engineering departments worldwide. The customer profile was deliberately diffuse: no single buyer held pricing leverage, and the installed base spanned aerospace contractors in the American Southwest, automotive electronics R&D centers in Bavaria, and university IEEE student chapters from Seoul to São Paulo.

The commercial logic was durable. A ProtoMat desktop mechanical milling system or a ProtoLaser UV unit represented a capital outlay of roughly €30,000 to €100,000 — modest against the cost of outsourcing prototype runs to Asian PCB houses, and trivially small against the delay cost if a design iteration missed a product launch window. Defense and aerospace customers in particular valued the self-sufficiency: classified circuit designs could stay behind the facility perimeter. LPKF's Garbsen headquarters and the network of regional subsidiaries maintained application support engineers who could walk a customer's lab technician through first-time setup, a service layer that reinforced retention and generated consumables revenue on routing bits, etch resist films, and process chemicals.

The segment was not high-growth by the time of the frozen snapshot. PCB prototyping was a mature category, and LPKF competed against desktop-format rivals for the lower end of the market while defending its position at the higher-precision tier. Revenue contribution from Development was meaningful but not the primary growth engine management pointed investors toward. What the segment provided was predictable cash flow, global brand recognition among working engineers, and a channel relationship that could in principle support cross-selling as LPKF's portfolio expanded into adjacent processes.

## Automotive Plastic Welding: The Tier-1 Supply Chain Relationship

The Welding segment told a different story — one tied closely to the automotive industry's multi-decade shift toward lightweight thermoplastic assemblies. Laser plastic welding joins two polymer components by transmitting a laser beam through one part and absorbing it at the interface, melting a precise seam without adhesives, solvents, or mechanical fasteners. For automotive applications — tail-lamp housings, fluid reservoir assemblies, sensor enclosures, ADAS module housings, and structural interior panels — the process offered clean geometry, hermetic seals, and compatibility with automated production lines running at automotive-scale throughput.

LPKF's LPKF PowerWeld and TwinWeld systems, along with the contour welding and simultaneous welding variants, found their primary buyers in the tier-1 and tier-2 automotive supply chain. Continental, Bosch, and the broader European lighting and plastics processing supply chain operated LPKF equipment, though LPKF's public disclosures did not enumerate named customers at the production site level. The strategic dynamic was that automotive OEMs specified laser welding processes, but the capital equipment purchase decision resided with the tier-1 or tier-2 molder or assembler who had to hit the OEM's quality and cycle-time spec.

The electric vehicle transition created a secondary demand layer. EV architectures carried more sealed electronic control units, battery management modules, and power electronics housings than their internal combustion equivalents, and each of those assemblies required a joining process. Laser plastic welding competed with ultrasonic welding and vibration welding in this space, with laser technology offering advantages in joint quality and process control visibility — arguments LPKF's application engineers made frequently to automotive procurement teams through the early 2020s.

Revenue from the Welding segment tracked automotive production volumes with a lag, meaning the supply chain disruptions of 2021-2022 created irregular order patterns that management acknowledged in investor communications. By 2023-2024, ~~as automotive production partially normalized, the segment returned to steadier order intake, though the broader European automotive demand softening — driven by the slower-than-projected EV uptake and inventory corrections at German OEMs — created renewed headwinds that management was navigating through the restructuring cycle~~ ==the segment was running at roughly €18.6 million in revenue with an adjusted EBIT of about €-4.8 million, as the broader European automotive demand softening — driven by the slower-than-projected EV uptake and inventory corrections at German OEMs — pushed Welding into loss-making territory that management was working to address through the restructuring cycle==.

## Laser Direct Structuring: The Smartphone Antenna Chapter and Its Aftermath

The Electronics segment's defining product line was Laser Direct Structuring (LDS), commercialized under the LPKF Multiline brand, which enabled circuit traces to be patterned directly onto three-dimensionally molded plastic parts. The technology created Molded Interconnect Devices (MIDs), and its most significant application was the integration of cellular antenna structures into smartphone housings and interior plastic frames.

The LDS antenna era shaped LPKF's financial trajectory through the 2013-2019 period. As smartphone OEMs crammed more frequency bands — and ultimately 5G sub-6GHz and millimeter-wave capability — into thinning handset profiles, LDS-structured three-dimensional antenna forms offered spatial efficiency that flat-antenna designs could not match. LPKF's systems processed the plastic substrates; LPKF's proprietary laser-activatable additive was compounded into the plastic; and the antenna patterns were then metallized by the contract manufacturer's plating line. The company's LDS equipment and materials were integrated into the supply chains of antenna component suppliers serving multiple major handset brands.

The segment's revenue, however, proved volatile. As handset makers standardized their antenna designs and competing processes — flexible printed circuits, direct printing — gained traction, LDS pricing came under pressure and capital equipment order patterns became lumpy. LPKF invested in broadening LDS applications into medical device interconnects, industrial IoT sensor housings, and automotive radar modules, but none of those adjacencies replicated the volume density that smartphone antenna had provided at its peak. By the mid-2020s, the Electronics segment was a stable contributor rather than a high-growth engine, with LPKF positioning LDS in its investor materials primarily as a technology demonstrating the company's core competence in laser-materials interaction rather than a primary revenue growth driver.

## LIDE: The Glass Substrate Option

Against that backdrop of mature-segment stability, LPKF's most consequential strategic development heading into the late 2020s was Laser Induced Deep Etching — LIDE. The process uses ultrashort-pulse laser exposure followed by a wet chemical etch to create high-aspect-ratio microstructures in glass substrates: through-glass vias, precision cavities, and shaped glass panels with tolerances measured in single-digit microns.

The commercial opportunity LPKF's management articulated was the semiconductor industry's nascent shift toward glass core substrates for advanced packaging. Organic substrates — the laminate boards on which logic dies and memory packages are assembled in high-performance processors and AI accelerators — faced physical limits in routing density and thermal performance. Glass, with superior dimensional stability, lower coefficient of thermal expansion, and electrical properties compatible with high-speed signaling, had attracted the attention of major semiconductor companies exploring next-generation packaging architectures.

LPKF's Vitrion ~~partnership~~ ==operation== was the primary vehicle for scaling LIDE toward that commercial inflection. Vitrion ~~was structured as a separate entity~~ ==functioned as LPKF's in-house glass-processing center of excellence and foundry== to accelerate glass substrate development and engage directly with advanced packaging customers and their supply chain partners, ~~reducing the organizational friction of operating a speculative, capital-intensive development program inside a €100-million-revenue specialty equipment company~~ ==housing the speculative, capital-intensive development program within LPKF's roughly €115-million-revenue specialty equipment footprint==.

LPKF's Garbsen facility housed the LIDE technology development and early production capability. The manufacturing footprint in Garbsen — the headquarters site that had served as the company's primary engineering and production base ~~for decades~~ ==since the 1991 move to Garbsen== — thus carried dual responsibility: sustaining the existing PCB prototyping, welding, and electronics equipment businesses while hosting the advanced glass processing work that management believed could become a disproportionate contributor to enterprise value over a multi-year horizon.

## Germany Manufacturing: Garbsen as the Hub

The Garbsen facility, situated in the Hannover metropolitan area in Lower Saxony, reflected LPKF's roots as a precision engineering company embedded in Germany's Mittelstand industrial tradition. The site combined mechanical engineering, laser optics assembly, process application laboratories, and global customer support operations within a campus that had expanded incrementally as the product portfolio grew.

LPKF complemented Garbsen with regional subsidiaries in North America, Asia-Pacific, and elsewhere, primarily organized as sales and application support operations rather than manufacturing centers. The production concentration in Germany meant that Garbsen-based engineering and manufacturing costs were denominated in euros and subject to German labor market dynamics — a structural consideration that the 2023-2024 operational restructuring program addressed through headcount and process efficiency initiatives management communicated to Frankfurt Xetra investors in their restructuring disclosures.

The strategic logic of maintaining German manufacturing — rather than pursuing Asian production-cost arbitrage — rested on the precision-engineering content of LPKF's systems and the intellectual property embedded in laser optics, control software, and process recipes that would be difficult to protect at arm's-length contract manufacturing relationships. For LIDE specifically, the technology sensitivity reinforced the case for keeping production capability close to the Garbsen engineering center through the commercial development phase.

chapters.title: Where LPKF sits in laser micromachining, PCB prototyping, glass processing
chapters.body:
## A Specialist in a Field of Giants

LPKF Laser & Electronics occupies an unusual address in the industrial landscape: a mid-cap specialist wedged between the enormous diversified laser houses and a scatter of niche players, holding dominant or near-dominant positions in markets small enough that the giants rarely bother to show up. The Garbsen company's three principal competitive theatres — laser micromachining systems broadly, benchtop PCB prototyping, and the nascent glass-substrate processing market underpinned by its LIDE technology — each have distinct competitive dynamics, and in each, LPKF's positioning tells a different story about moat depth and growth durability.

## Laser Micromachining: Competing Where Trumpf Does Not

The laser industry's topography begins with the equipment titans. Trumpf, LPKF's compatriot and the world's largest laser machine builder, commands the cutting, welding, and additive-manufacturing space at industrial scale. IPG Photonics dominates high-power fibre-laser sources. Coherent, assembled from the 2022 merger with II-VI, spans everything from semiconductor lasers to ultrafast amplifiers. None of these companies regard LPKF as a primary competitor: their revenue bases dwarf LPKF's annual turnover, and their focus lies in kilowatt-range industrial processing, not the sub-100-micron precision regime where LPKF operates.

In the micromachining specialty — defined roughly as laser ablation, structuring, drilling, and cutting at feature sizes from a few microns to a few hundred microns — the competitive set narrows sharply. The most directly comparable publicly visible rival is **LASEA**, the Belgian ultrafast-laser micromachining specialist headquartered in Liège. LASEA built its reputation in watchmaking components, medical-device microfabrication, and microelectronics, deploying femtosecond and picosecond laser platforms in markets that require tight dimensional tolerances and minimal heat-affected zones. LASEA remains private, which limits public disclosure; the company's revenue scale is believed to be well below LPKF's, and its geographic reach is primarily European and Swiss-tier. The two companies overlap on precision drilling and surface structuring in electronics applications, but LASEA's niche gravity pulls toward luxury and medtech rather than the semiconductor-packaging and consumer-electronics substrate markets that LPKF is now targeting.

**3D-Micromac**, based in Chemnitz and also private, represents a closer structural parallel. The company focuses on laser micromachining for photovoltaic cell processing, display glass scribing, and wafer dicing — segments that intersect with LPKF's solar and development activities. Their ScribeLineTM thin-film scribing systems competed directly with LPKF's solar laser tools during the thin-film PV boom, and both companies navigated the solar market's painful contraction post-2012. 3D-Micromac's pivot toward roll-to-roll processing and display glass has taken it in a direction tangential to LPKF's current strategy.

**MKS Instruments**, through its Electro Scientific Industries (ESI) acquisition, brings meaningful scale to laser drilling and processing for printed-circuit boards and consumer electronics. ESI's UV laser drilling systems have long served the HDI PCB market for via formation in mass production — a high-volume, cost-sensitive segment where LPKF does not compete. The overlap narrows to certain laser-direct-structuring applications where both companies offer tools for additive conductive-trace formation on moulded substrates, though LPKF's LDS process carries a proprietary dimension through its patents on selective metallisation of laser-activated areas on thermoplastic substrates.

What distinguishes LPKF within this micromachining constellation is the combination of vertical application focus and process-IP moat. LDS — Laser Direct Structuring, applied to three-dimensional moulded interconnect devices — remains LPKF's most durable competitive asset in electronics. The process, in which a laser selectively activates a catalyst-doped polymer surface to enable selective copper plating, underpins the antenna-in-housing designs prevalent in mobile devices, hearing aids, and automotive radar sensors. Competitors have attempted to develop analogous direct-structuring chemistries, but LPKF's patent portfolio and its co-development relationships with resin suppliers have maintained meaningful barriers. Revenue from LDS systems and licence arrangements has, historically, been the electronics segment's primary driver, though unit volumes are sensitive to the consumer-electronics capex cycle.

## PCB Prototyping: Dominant in a Shrinking Room

The benchtop PCB prototyping market presents a more complicated picture. LPKF's ProtoMat systems have for decades been the instrument of choice in university electronics labs, corporate R&D departments, and defence contractors that require rapid, in-house circuit-board iteration without depending on external fabrication services. The company claims dominant share in this segment globally, a position enabled by its combination of mechanical milling capability, laser structuring options, and an ecosystem of software (CircuitPro) designed for the electronics engineer rather than the fabrication specialist.

The structural headwind is plain. The emergence of low-cost Asian PCB fabrication services — with online platforms offering two-day turnaround on two-layer boards for single-digit dollars — has materially compressed the economic case for in-house prototyping at small quantities. For startups and university labs working on standard FR4 designs, the calculus has tilted toward outsourcing even early iterations. LPKF's response has been to emphasise the segments where in-house prototyping retains operational necessity: classified defence programmes where exporting design files is prohibited; applications requiring same-day or same-hour iteration cycles; and advanced-substrate work — flexible circuits, high-frequency PTFE laminates, and multilayer constructions — where standard fabs require minimum quantities or long lead times.

The competitive roster in this niche is thin. **T-Tech** (US) and **MITS Electronics** (Japan) manufacture competing benchtop milling and routing systems, but neither has matched LPKF's global installed base, software integration, or dealer network depth. The risk to LPKF is less competitive displacement than secular volume attrition: an installed base that renews slowly, with new unit sales dependent on the formation of new R&D programmes rather than replacement cycles.

## Glass Substrates: The Open Field

The competitive terrain shifts entirely when LPKF's LIDE technology is considered. LIDE — Laser Induced Deep Etching — is a two-step process in which ultrafast laser pulses create damage tracks through glass at high aspect ratios, which are then developed by wet chemical etch into precision through-glass vias (TGVs) and patterned features. The technology is aimed at the emerging glass-core substrate market for semiconductor advanced packaging, where the industry is exploring glass as an alternative to the organic laminates that have served as the foundation of high-density interconnect packages for two decades.

Intel's 2023 disclosure of its glass-core substrate roadmap, targeting production deployment toward 2030 for leading-edge chip packages, functioned as a market-formation signal for the entire supply chain. Glass offers advantages that are difficult to match with organic: near-zero moisture absorption, thermal expansion coefficients that can be engineered closer to silicon, surface flatness superior to most organic options at ultra-high via densities, and compatibility with thinner package profiles. The trade-offs are real — glass is brittle, processing yields at scale remain to be proven in high-volume manufacturing, and the capital intensity of transitioning a packaging line from organic to glass is substantial.

The competitive set facing LPKF in glass processing is heterogeneous. **Chemical etching** — principally hydrofluoric acid wet processes — can produce through-glass structures, but struggles to achieve the via densities (pitches below 100 microns) and tight diameter tolerances required for advanced packaging interconnects without expensive photolithographic masking steps. Laser alternatives include **stealth dicing and damage-track** approaches from companies including **Hamamatsu Photonics**, which has developed laser processing tools for glass scribing and via formation, and **Photon Dynamics / Applied Materials** group tools oriented toward display glass. None, as of the frozen snapshot date, has demonstrated at commercial scale the via aspect ratios and density specifications that LIDE targets.

~~LPKF's partnership with **Vitrion** represents~~ ==**Vitrion**, LPKF's in-house glass-processing center of excellence and foundry, represents== the principal vehicle through which LIDE transitions from a machine-sale proposition to a substrate-supply one. By ~~positioning Vitrion as a glass-substrate manufacturer deploying LIDE-equipped production lines~~ ==operating Vitrion as a captive LIDE foundry supplying processed glass substrates==, LPKF seeks participation in the substrate value chain beyond the one-time equipment transaction — a model that carries higher recurring revenue potential but also concentrates execution risk on a single ~~commercial-scale proof point~~ ==internal commercial-scale proof point==. The success of that proof point will determine whether LIDE remains a differentiated technology asset or becomes a laboratory achievement that larger players replicate once the market scales beyond its pioneering stage.

| Processing approach | Via density capability | LPKF competitive read |
|---|---|---|
| HF chemical etch (no laser) | Low–moderate; litho masking required | Limited at high density |
| Laser drilling (nanosecond UV) | Moderate; taper and HAZ challenges | Commoditising |
| LPKF LIDE (ultrafast + etch) | High; sub-50 µm pitch demonstrated | Proprietary; unproven at volume |
| Hamamatsu damage-track scribing | Moderate | Primarily display/scribing focus |

The competitive position LPKF holds going into 2026 is, in sum, one of differentiated technology awaiting commercial validation. In laser micromachining and PCB prototyping, its moats are real but sized to markets that do not excite large-scale competitors. In glass substrates, it has arrived early at what may prove to be a significant inflection in semiconductor packaging — carrying proprietary process IP and ~~a partner vehicle~~ ==a captive foundry vehicle== for scaling, but facing a validation timeline that has consistently slipped to the right across the industry.

chapters.title: Timeline from 1976 through LIDE positioning
chapters.body:
## The Founding Arc: Laser Precision from Bench to Bourse

Fifty years before the semiconductor industry began reckoning with the limits of organic substrates, ~~a small engineering enterprise took shape in Garbsen, a quiet industrial suburb west of Hannover. LPKF Laser & Electronics was established in 1976~~ ==a small engineering enterprise was founded on 4 August 1976, only later relocating to its Garbsen headquarters west of Hannover in 1991. LPKF Laser & Electronics was established== with a narrow mandate: building precision tools for printed circuit board prototyping, then a laborious process conducted largely by hand. The company's early products — mechanical routing and milling machines for PCB layouts — addressed a genuine engineering pain point, allowing electronics designers to iterate rapidly without committing to expensive batch fabrication runs.

Through the 1980s and into the 1990s, LPKF refined its prototyping equipment, earning a loyal base of customers among university research departments, automotive electronics suppliers, and corporate R&D labs across Europe and North America. The pivot to laser-based processing came as semiconductor geometries shrank and the PCB traces that connected them shrank with them — demanding precision that mechanical tools could no longer reliably deliver. Lasers offered non-contact, repeatable ablation at micron-level tolerances, and LPKF invested in the optics and control software needed to translate that physics into production-ready tools. By the time the company listed on the Frankfurt Stock Exchange — eventually ~~joining the SDAX index of smaller German industrials~~ ==securing a brief membership of the SDAX index of smaller German industrials between December 2024 and December 2025== — it had established itself as the principal German specialist in laser micromachining for electronics manufacturing.

## The Laser Direct Structuring Era: A Decade of Smartphone-Driven Growth

The technology that would define LPKF's most expansive chapter was Laser Direct Structuring, or LDS. Developed through the late 1990s and early 2000s, LDS enabled circuit traces to be written directly onto three-dimensional plastic substrates — so-called molded interconnect devices — by doping the plastic with a metallic additive, selectively activating it with a laser, and electroplating the exposed tracks to conductivity. The process embedded antennas, sensors, and interconnects directly into device housings, eliminating discrete antenna modules and recovering precious interior volume in an era of fierce dimensional competition.

Smartphone manufacturers discovered LDS in earnest around 2010. Nokia became an early high-profile adopter, integrating LDS antennas into its Lumia handset line; other original equipment manufacturers followed as the technology demonstrated its value. LPKF's Electronics segment — supplying LDS laser systems globally — swelled accordingly, driving revenue toward the upper bound of the company's historical range and making LDS the dominant earnings contributor through the early part of the following decade.

The dependency carried latent risk. As the smartphone market matured and OEM designs converged on a narrower set of manufacturing choices, LDS adoption plateaued. The technology remained embedded in automotive and industrial applications — radar sensors, hearing aids, medical devices — but the explosive handset-driven volume growth did not persist. Revenue contracted from its mid-decade highs, and LPKF entered a more difficult period of margin compression and strategic re-evaluation.

## Restructuring and Strategic Refocus (2019–2024)

Under Klaus Fiedler as chief executive, LPKF began rationalising its four operating segments — Development, Electronics, Solar, and Welding — while simultaneously investing in what would become its most consequential technological bet. The Solar segment, which had supplied laser ablation tools for thin-film and crystalline silicon cell manufacturers, faced persistent headwinds as Chinese solar manufacturing scaled and equipment pricing compressed. The Welding segment, serving automotive and industrial laser plastic-joining applications, offered steadier but modest growth. Formal restructuring through 2023 and 2024 aimed to pare costs and redirect engineering resources toward higher-margin opportunities.

Revenue held in a range consistent with the company's SDAX-scale positioning — broadly in the €100m-to-€150m band — without the step-change growth that would rerate the shares materially. Investors tracking the Frankfurt-listed LPK.DE observed a company in measured transition: operationally cautious, balance-sheet managed, but carrying an asset that conventional segment analysis did not fully price.

## LIDE: Writing Through Glass

That asset was LIDE — Laser Induced Deep Etching. The technology exploited ultrafast laser interaction with glass substrates to create high-aspect-ratio through-glass vias and precision cuts with exceptional sidewall quality. Where conventional mechanical or wet-chemical approaches to glass processing produced rough edges and geometric imprecision ill-suited to semiconductor-grade specifications, LIDE enabled micron-level via geometries compatible with the metallisation schemes that advanced packaging foundries and outsourced assembly and test providers required. The process was non-contact, scalable to panel formats, and produced via structures whose dimensional tolerances rivalled anything available through competing glass-processing routes.

The catalyst for renewed investor attention arrived from outside LPKF itself. As leading semiconductor companies — Intel prominently among them — disclosed roadmaps for glass core substrates as successors to organic laminates in high-performance compute and AI accelerator packaging, the structural case for LIDE sharpened considerably. Glass cores promised lower signal loss at high frequencies, superior dimensional stability over temperature cycling, and a coefficient of thermal expansion closer to silicon than organic alternatives — material advantages in the sub-micron interconnect regimes demanded by heterogeneous chiplet architectures. LPKF's through-glass via capability, delivered at production-relevant throughputs via LIDE, positioned the company as a potential equipment vendor at the intersection of two long-cycle trends: the advanced packaging buildout and the transition to panel-level manufacturing formats.

To accelerate LIDE's path to commercial scale, LPKF ~~structured the Vitrion partnership — an arrangement designed to marry its laser processing expertise with~~ ==established Vitrion as its in-house glass-processing center of excellence and foundry, pairing its laser processing expertise with== the substrate-level commercialisation infrastructure needed to satisfy semiconductor supply chains that require high-volume, qualified process guarantors rather than laboratory demonstrators.

## Forward Catalysts: The Inflection Window

By the frozen snapshot of May 2026, two catalysts defined LPKF's near-term trajectory. The first and more transformative was LIDE's commercial inflection: whether glass core substrates would graduate from foundry roadmap commitments to volume equipment orders placed with process-tool suppliers. Industry timelines had consistently signalled a 2026-to-2028 window for early glass substrate production ramps, making the current period a critical qualification phase. A confirmed volume tool placement from a tier-one advanced packaging customer — or ~~a financing or strategic event signalling Vitrion's commercialisation progress~~ ==a qualified customer engagement or process milestone at LPKF's Vitrion glass-processing foundry== — would constitute the most material near-term catalyst the stock had carried in a decade.

The second catalyst was more prosaic but no less important to near-term earnings: stabilisation and recovery in the core Development and Electronics segments. PCB prototyping remained a recurring-revenue, consumables-supported business with defensive characteristics; the LDS electronics segment, while far from its smartphone-era peak, retained exposure to automotive electrification and industrial automation programmes that were expanding, not contracting.

Taken together, LPKF's fifty-year arc from ~~Garbsen PCB workshop to SDAX-listed precision laser specialist~~ ==regional PCB workshop to Frankfurt-listed precision laser specialist== had deposited the company at an unusual juncture — modest in current revenue scale, specific in its technological moat, and carrying optionality on a structural shift in semiconductor packaging whose timing, if not its ultimate direction, remained genuinely uncertain.

chapters.title: LIDE IP, laser micromachining IP, patent portfolio
chapters.body:
## The Architecture of a Laser IP Estate

Fifty years of precision engineering left LPKF Laser & Electronics SE with something most mid-cap German industrialists quietly envy: a proprietary technology catalogue assembled through decades of incremental innovation, where each product generation funded the next layer of intellectual property. By the frozen snapshot date of May 2026, that estate rested on two distinct but reinforcing pillars — the mature licensing engine of Laser Direct Structuring and the emerging, strategically critical claims staked around Laser Induced Deep Etching (LIDE) for glass substrates.

## LIDE: Filing Around a Process, Not Just a Machine

LIDE's patent architecture reflects how LPKF approached the glass processing opportunity: not merely as a capital equipment provider selling a tool, but as the inventor of a method that controls the full process chain. The core LIDE mechanism couples an ultrashort-pulse (USP) laser — operating in the picosecond to femtosecond range — with a selective wet-chemical etch, typically hydrofluoric acid chemistry. The laser modifies the glass lattice along precisely defined filament paths without ablating material outright; the subsequent etch then attacks only the modified zones, leaving surrounding glass structurally intact. The combination produces through-holes and cavities with aspect ratios exceeding 20:1, tolerances measured in single-digit micrometres, and smooth sidewalls unsuitable for competing techniques including mechanical micro-drilling or standard CO₂ ablation.

The IP scope accordingly covers both the laser parameter space — pulse duration, repetition rate, focal geometry, beam shaping — and the process chemistry that determines etch selectivity. Patents filed in this domain since the mid-2010s addressed a manufacturing reality: any competitor replicating LIDE functionality would need to solve the same coupled problem of filament formation and selective removal, making freedom-to-operate difficult without crossing into LPKF's filed territory. The company extended its claims into throughput architectures, including multi-beam and stepped-wafer processing approaches relevant to panel-level packaging at the dimensions semiconductor advanced packaging customers require.

~~Vitrion, the joint-venture vehicle LPKF assembled to pursue~~ ==Vitrion, LPKF's in-house glass-processing centre of excellence and foundry service for== glass core substrate commercialisation, provided an additional mechanism: IP ~~contributed to the venture~~ ==housed within the foundry== carried protective overlay for the combined process stack, while ~~the partnership structure allowed manufacturing know-how transfer~~ ==operating LIDE production directly let LPKF scale manufacturing know-how== without diluting ~~LPKF's~~ ==its== core patent positions.

## LDS: A Licensing Model That Proved the Template

Laser Direct Structuring supplied the proof of concept that LIDE investors and observers examined most carefully. LPKF had pioneered LDS — the two-stage process of laser-activating a proprietary additive embedded in injection-moulded polymer, then selectively metallising the activated zones — in the late 1990s and early 2000s. Patent protection on the core LDS method, the laser-activatable material chemistry (developed in collaboration with material partners), and the metallisation sequence built a licensing estate that generated recurring royalty income from every LDS-equipped production line installed outside LPKF's own equipment sales.

The LDS licensing model demonstrated that LPKF could extract value beyond equipment hardware, collecting per-part or per-run royalties as the antenna and sensor applications built on LDS technology scaled into hundreds of millions of units annually in consumer electronics. That revenue stream buffered cyclical swings in equipment demand and validated the company's approach of building IP rather than settling for process-equipment supplier status. When LIDE's semiconductor packaging opportunity began attracting serious industry attention through 2023–2025, management pointed to LDS licensing's margin profile as the appropriate financial analogy for what a mature LIDE position might eventually generate.

## The Broader Laser Micromachining Estate

Beyond LIDE and LDS, LPKF's filed portfolio reached across its four operating segments. Laser plastic welding — the Welding segment's core — carried claims around contour and quasi-simultaneous welding geometries, along with the optical delivery systems that enable through-transmission joining at the tolerances automotive and medical device customers demand. PCB prototyping and rapid-routing tools, commercialised since the 1990s, were protected by claims on laser parameter selection for dielectric materials, mechanical handling integration, and the software-controlled process sequencing that competitors reverse-engineering the hardware could not trivially reproduce.

The cumulative result was a portfolio spanning materials types — glass, polymer, semiconductor, metallic interconnect layers — and wavelength regimes from UV excimer to near-IR solid-state to the ultrashort-pulse domain. Breadth of that kind is defensively useful: a customer evaluating LPKF against a specialist rival in any single application confronted not just a machine comparison but a licensing exposure question.

## R&D Organisation and Investment Discipline

LPKF maintained its primary R&D operations at the Garbsen headquarters campus outside Hannover, where process development, systems engineering and applications laboratories shared physical proximity. A US technology centre in Wilsonville, Oregon, served the North American semiconductor and electronics customer base and provided an outpost for engaging with advanced packaging ecosystem partners operating on Pacific time.

Collaboration with Fraunhofer institutes, particularly in optics and photonics, gave LPKF access to applied-research capacity without carrying the full cost of basic science infrastructure. Joint development agreements structured with such partners typically allowed LPKF to retain exclusive commercial licensing rights to resulting IP, a model common among well-managed German Mittelstand technology companies with histories of successful academic technology transfer.

R&D investment across the restructuring years of 2023 and 2024 remained elevated relative to revenue as the company deliberately funded LIDE process refinement and the engineering work required to bring glass substrate processing to the panel dimensions advanced packaging customers specified. That decision — to protect the technology investment cycle even as topline revenue contracted — reflected management's calculation that the LIDE window of competitive advantage was finite and front-loading the patent estate would determine whether LPKF entered the glass substrate era as a licensor or merely a toll-road equipment vendor. The distinction carried substantial long-run margin implications for every scenario in which glass core substrates achieved material penetration in AI and high-performance computing packaging stacks.

chapters.title: LIDE commercial uncertainty, segment cyclicality, FX, competitive, governance, scale
chapters.body:
## The Spectrum of Structural Risk

For a company whose equity story rests on a technology that has not yet generated material revenue, the principal risk sits squarely in the gap between proof of concept and commercial scale. LPKF Laser & Electronics entered its fifth decade as a Garbsen-based specialty systems house with ~~roughly €100–150 million~~ ==roughly €115–125 million== in annual revenue across four operating segments, ~~an SDAX listing on Frankfurt Xetra~~ ==a Frankfurt Xetra listing that exited SDAX effective 22 December 2025==, and a balance sheet strained by the restructuring actions of 2023 and 2024. The combination of execution risk in LIDE glass processing, cyclicality in the legacy segments, foreign-exchange translation drag, intensifying competition, thin governance protections, and capital scarcity creates a layered risk profile that investors must disaggregate before assigning probability weights to the bull case.

---

## LIDE: The Inflection Clock

The most consequential uncertainty facing LPKF through the 2026–2028 window was the timing of commercial inflection for its Laser Induced Deep Etching technology. LIDE promised a pathway into the semiconductor advanced-packaging glass core substrate market — a segment that analysts at firms including SEMI and Yole Développement had identified as one of the more structurally durable growth themes in the broader semiconductor supply chain. Glass substrates offered lower dielectric loss, tighter dimensional stability, and superior thermal performance relative to conventional organic alternatives, and the hyperscale compute buildout — driven by AI inference and training chips — was adding urgency to the packaging transition.

The problem for LPKF was sequencing. The company had invested in LIDE development and ~~established a partnership framework with Vitrion~~ ==built out its Vitrion glass-processing center of excellence== to address glass market scaling, but as of the frozen snapshot date of 23 May 2026 the technology had not yet demonstrated the kind of high-volume, high-yield throughput that major semiconductor outsourced assembly and test customers require before committing to equipment purchase orders at scale. The capital cycle in advanced packaging is long: customers qualify processes over twelve to thirty-six months before any revenue appears on a supplier's order book. LPKF's small revenue base — a fraction of what peers such as Coherent or SCREEN Holdings generated across their respective product families — meant it had limited cushion if the inflection arrived later than consensus expected. Each quarter of delay extended the period during which the company was effectively funding LIDE development through cash generated by slower-growth legacy segments. Management had guided toward commercial progress but had stopped short of hard delivery milestones that investors could hold them to. That studied ambiguity was itself a risk signal.

---

## Segment Cyclicality

The four operating segments that generated the cash supporting LIDE development each carried their own cyclical exposures. The Development segment — centred on PCB prototyping and rapid PCB systems — was tightly correlated with electronics research and development investment cycles. When semiconductor design activity slowed, as it did episodically through the 2023–2024 inventory correction, development tooling budgets contracted quickly and disproportionately; capital expenditure on prototyping equipment is discretionary in ways that production tooling is not.

The Electronics segment, which included laser direct structuring systems for molded interconnect devices, carried meaningful automotive end-market exposure. LDS technology had found its largest adoption in automotive antenna and sensor integration, and the automotive cycle through 2023–2025 was characterised by hesitation: OEMs were navigating electric-vehicle transition costs, production rescheduling, and a softening of the consumer order rate in key European and Chinese markets. LPKF's welding segment compounded this concentration — laser plastic welding drew heavily from automotive module assembly, meaning that a sustained automotive downturn hit two of the four operating segments simultaneously.

Solar offered a different cyclical profile but not a less volatile one. Solar cell processing demand tracked government subsidy regimes, installation incentive schedules, and the competitive cost curve of Chinese panel manufacturers. LPKF's legacy solar equipment had faced persistent margin compression as Chinese domestic laser equipment producers moved up the value chain, and while the segment contributed to revenue it did not provide the stability that would have buffered LIDE investment spending.

---

## Foreign Exchange and EUR Translation

LPKF reported in euros and generated the majority of its corporate costs in euros, but its customer base was genuinely global — spanning European electronics manufacturers, North American PCB prototyping shops, and increasingly Asian semiconductor packaging customers. Revenue booked in US dollars, South Korean won, Japanese yen, or Chinese renminbi all translated back to euros at prevailing exchange rates, and the euro's trajectory against the dollar through 2024 and into 2025 had been volatile enough to introduce meaningful translation noise into reported figures. A one-cent move in the EUR/USD rate against a comparable prior-period average could shift reported revenue by several hundred thousand euros on a base of this scale, and hedging capacity at LPKF's size was structurally limited relative to a large-cap industrial exporter with dedicated treasury operations. The FX overlay was particularly relevant for LIDE revenue if and when it arrived: semiconductor packaging customers in Taiwan and South Korea would almost certainly negotiate contracts denominated in US dollars or local currency, adding translation exposure at precisely the moment LPKF would most need clean revenue comparisons to validate the technology story to Frankfurt equity investors.

---

## Competitive Intensity

LPKF occupied a defensible niche in laser micromachining but it was not uncontested. In PCB prototyping, the company held a market-leading position built over decades, but competitors including LPKF's historical German peers and several Asian systems integrators continued to attack the segment on price. In glass processing — the forward growth arena — the competitive horizon was wider and the incumbents more formidable. Corning's internal processing capabilities, partnerships involving Coherent's ultrashort-pulse laser platforms, and emerging work from Asian laser OEMs targeting the same advanced-packaging glass market all represented credible threats. LASEA, the Belgian precision laser specialist, competed in overlapping ultrafast-laser micromachining applications. The distinguishing claim for LIDE was its specific process window for through-glass via formation and panel-level scribing, but intellectual property in laser micromachining is susceptible to design-around, and a well-capitalised competitor with deep application engineering resources could close the gap faster than the LPKF balance sheet could maintain a development lead.

---

## Governance and ~~SDAX~~ ==Post-SDAX== Small-Cap Status

~~LPKF's SDAX membership placed~~ ==LPKF's removal from SDAX effective 22 December 2025 placed== it in a segment of the Frankfurt market characterised by lower daily trading liquidity, narrower analyst coverage, and structural underrepresentation in passive flows relative to MDAX or DAX constituents. As of the snapshot date, the company operated under Germany's two-tier supervisory board structure, which provided meaningful stakeholder representation but also meant that activist influence over strategic pivots was mediated through board channels rather than direct shareholder pressure. The combination of small float, thin sell-side coverage, and a technology story that required patient capital created a valuation environment where sentiment could move the stock well beyond fundamental anchor points in either direction. Periods of semiconductor packaging enthusiasm tended to pull LPKF's multiple sharply higher; periods of sector-level scepticism could detach it from any reasonable intrinsic value estimate. That reflexivity was both an opportunity and a governance risk: management operated with limited external discipline on capital allocation.

---

## Scale and Capital Constraints

The synthesis of the above risks converged on a single structural constraint: size. With a revenue base ~~at the lower end of the €100–150 million range~~ ==of roughly €115 million in FY2025==, LPKF had to fund LIDE development, maintain competitive R&D investment across its legacy segments, service any restructuring obligations from the 2023–2024 programme, and sustain a sales and applications engineering organisation capable of qualifying a new class of semiconductor packaging customers — all simultaneously. The capital requirements of glass substrate process development were not trivial; tool qualification alone at major OSAT or IDM facilities could demand co-investment, field application support, and performance guarantees that stressed the working capital of a company of this scale. Equity issuance would dilute existing shareholders into a market where the story remained unproven; debt capacity was constrained by earnings volatility. The path through the inflection required LPKF to remain solvent and credible long enough for LIDE adoption to accelerate — a window that, in semiconductor capital equipment cycles, had historically been measured in years rather than quarters.

chapters.title: The next 12 months — catalysts, estimates, and what to watch
chapters.body:
## The reporting calendar, annotated

LPKF's Frankfurt Xetra cadence is thinner than American quarterly feeds but maps neatly onto the next twelve months. Working forward from the frozen snapshot of 23 May 2026, ~~five~~ ==six== discrete dates structure the investment timeline.

The **Annual General Meeting** — ~~most likely falling in late June 2026~~ ==scheduled for 4 June 2026== — is the first formal inflection point. Shareholders will receive the FY2025 dividend confirmation and, more importantly for thesis-trackers, management's first open-microphone session since the full-year results. LIDE commercialisation progress and ~~Vitrion partnership~~ ==Vitrion glass-foundry== milestones will dominate the Q&A.

The **H1 2026 interim report**, ~~typically published in mid-August~~ ==scheduled for 23 July 2026==, delivers the first hard half-year data on whether the post-restructuring revenue ~~recovery is sustaining pace or losing momentum~~ ==trajectory is stabilising or stepping down further from the FY2025 EUR 115.3 M base==. This is the report where a meaningful LIDE revenue line — even a small one — would constitute a step-change in how the market models the business.

~~Between August and year-end there is limited formal disclosure.~~ ==The **Q3 2026 statement** on 29 October 2026 is the next hard disclosure after the H1 report, covering nine-month order intake and segment trajectory.== Watch for any **capital-markets or technology day** that management may schedule; LPKF has historically used these events to update institutional investors on LIDE programme milestones, and a customer-qualification announcement could arrive through an ad hoc Frankfurt Xetra disclosure at any time.

**Preliminary FY2026 figures** typically land in late January 2027, followed by the **full annual report and FY2027 guidance** in March 2027. That March report will be the first occasion on which management can credibly frame LIDE's contribution to the medium-term revenue profile — or, in the bear case, defer that framing yet again.

---

## Consensus estimates: the numbers as they stood

LPKF covers a narrow sell-side universe, typically three to five German mid-cap analysts at houses including Berenberg, Hauck Aufhäuser, and mwb research. The following table synthesises the consensus range as of the frozen snapshot, anchored to the FY2025 results management reported in Q1 2026.

| Period | Revenue (EUR, consensus midpoint) | YoY growth | EBIT margin (consensus) |
|---|---|---|---|
| FY2025A | ~~€138 M~~ ==€115.3 M== | ~~+28 % vs FY2024 trough~~ ==-6.2 % vs FY2024== | ~~7 %~~ ==~0.7 % adjusted (€0.8 M adjusted EBIT)== |
| FY2026E ==(company guidance)== | ~~€158 M~~ ==€105-120 M== | ~~+15 %~~ ==-9 % to +4 %== | ~~10 %~~ ==-3.0 % to +4.5 % adjusted== |
| FY2027E (base, no LIDE inflection) | ~~€175 M~~ ==sell-side consensus being reset post-FY2025 print== | ~~+11 %~~ ==n/m== | ~~12 %~~ ==n/m== |
| FY2027E (bull, LIDE ramp) | ~~€200 M+~~ ==contingent on a first volume LIDE order, still absent== | ~~+29 %+~~ ==n/m== | ~~15 %+~~ ==n/m== |

*Sources: Frankfurt Xetra disclosures for LPK.DE; LPKF Investor Relations; sell-side consensus as of May 2026. FY2025A figures as reported in the FY2025 annual report. Forward estimates are pre-tax operating measures; LPKF does not provide formal EPS guidance.*

~~The implied FY2026 growth of ~15 per cent rests on three pillars: a continued recovery in the Electronics segment (laser direct structuring demand from consumer and automotive MID applications), stabilisation in the Welding segment after several soft automotive-adjacent quarters, and a modest initial revenue contribution from LIDE glass processing.~~ ==The FY2026 guidance midpoint implies a low-single-digit decline from FY2025, with the upper end of the range only modestly above 2025 actuals. The three swing factors are: trajectory in the Electronics segment (laser direct structuring demand from consumer and automotive MID applications), stabilisation in the Welding segment after a loss-making FY2025 print, and any initial revenue contribution from LIDE glass processing.== ~~The EBIT margin expansion from roughly seven per cent to ten per cent assumes operating leverage on a largely fixed cost base, with restructuring one-offs fully absorbed by end-FY2025.~~ ==The adjusted EBIT margin guidance of -3.0 % to +4.5 % brackets break-even and reflects how little operating leverage there is at this revenue level on a largely fixed cost base, even with restructuring one-offs fully absorbed by end-FY2025.==

> "We enter 2026 with a leaner, more focused organisation. Our core segments are returning to growth, and the LIDE programme has reached a stage of technical maturity where we are having substantive commercial discussions with potential first customers. We are cautiously optimistic about the trajectory for the full year."

*— LPKF Management Board, paraphrased from FY2025 results presentation, February 2026. [LPKF Investor Relations](https://www.lpkf.com/en/investor-relations)*

Management's formal FY2026 guidance issued alongside the annual report set a revenue range of ~~**€145–165 million**~~ ==**€105-120 million**== and an ~~EBIT margin corridor of **8–11 per cent**~~ ==adjusted EBIT margin corridor of **-3.0 % to +4.5 %**==. The width of that range — ~~€20 million, roughly 13 per cent of the midpoint~~ ==€15 million, roughly 13 per cent of the midpoint== — reflects genuine uncertainty around LIDE timing rather than conservatism about the core business.

---

## Quarter-by-quarter: what confirms or breaks the thesis

**H1 2026 (report: ~~mid-August 2026~~ ==23 July 2026==).** The primary confirmation signal is an Electronics segment order intake that sustains or exceeds the FY2025 H2 run-rate. A sequential step-up in the development/LIDE revenue line — even into the low single-digit millions — would be read as evidence that customer qualification cycles are completing. Watch for any comment on Vitrion ==foundry== capacity utilisation; a cryptic reference to "increasing utilisation" in the LIDE sub-segment is the kind of disclosure that has historically moved the stock on thin volume before analysts fully digest it.

A miss at H1 looks like: Electronics revenues flat or declining sequentially, with management citing "continued order caution from MID customers" — the language used during the 2023 trough — alongside no LIDE revenue and a guidance narrowing toward the lower bound of the ~~€145–165 million~~ ==€105-120 million== corridor.

**FY2026 preliminary (late January 2027).** The key question is whether ==adjusted== EBIT margin exits the year above or below ~~ten per cent~~ ==the +4.5 % upper bound of guidance==. A print at or above ~~ten per cent~~ ==that upper bound==, even without a LIDE revenue contribution, would confirm operational leverage is re-engaging ~~as top-line recovers~~ ==even with a flat-to-down top-line==. More critical: any first reference to a "customer pilot" or "series production qualification" in the LIDE context would be the single most meaningful data point in the dossier — it sets the clock on what could become a transformative revenue segment.

A miss looks like: revenue at or below ~~€150 million~~ ==€105 million (the lower bound of guidance) and an adjusted EBIT margin printing toward the -3.0 % floor== with management citing project delays or "extended customer evaluation timelines" for LIDE. In that scenario, the FY2027 consensus base case shifts out twelve months and the option value re-rates lower.

**FY2026 full results and FY2027 guidance (March 2027).** This is the definitive catalyst window. If LIDE has delivered even €5–10 million in programme revenue during FY2026, management can credibly frame FY2027 as a volume-ramp year. ~~The bull case FY2027 estimate of €200 million-plus requires LIDE to contribute €20–30 million incremental to the base; that in turn implies one or more semiconductor customers moving from qualification to purchase order.~~ ==Any bull case for FY2027 requires LIDE to contribute meaningful incremental revenue on top of the €105-120 M FY2026 base, which in turn implies one or more semiconductor customers moving from qualification to purchase order.== The March 2027 report is the earliest plausible moment for that framing.

---

## Beat versus miss: the asymmetry

**Beat conditions** are binary in nature. A core-business beat — Electronics outperforming on LDS tool orders, Welding recovering faster than expected from its FY2025 adjusted-EBIT loss — would push consensus FY2026 estimates toward the top of the guided range, implying perhaps ten to fifteen per cent share-price upside on multiple expansion. Unexciting, but real.

The non-linear beat is LIDE. A single disclosed design win or volume qualification from a Tier 1 semiconductor advanced packaging customer — an Intel Foundry Services, a Samsung SDI, a glass substrate integrator building panel-level packaging lines — would not merely beat the consensus estimate. It would invalidate the modelling framework entirely, because the consensus has no LIDE revenue in the FY2026 base case. The stock would re-rate on TAM expansion logic, not on the revenue line itself.

**Miss conditions** are slower but more corrosive. A second consecutive year of LIDE deferrals, combined with Electronics softness driven by MID application weakness in consumer electronics or EV cost-out pressure in automotive, would erode confidence in the post-restructuring recovery narrative. The ~~2023 trough — approximately €108 million in revenue —~~ ==FY2025 step-down to €115.3 million in revenue with €0.8 million adjusted EBIT, alongside the earlier 2020-2021 lows around €93-96 million,== demonstrated that LPKF's core business is cyclical and exposed to capex discretion at OEM customers.

---

## The bull and bear in twelve sentences each

**Bull.** The glass core substrate market is real, growing, and technically demanding; ~~LPKF and Vitrion hold~~ ==LPKF, through its in-house Vitrion glass-processing centre of excellence, holds== demonstrably superior LIDE drilling capability. Intel's glass core roadmap, announced publicly in 2023 and substantiated by subsequent packaging conference presentations, creates a named, traceable customer pull. At least one design win in the next twelve months is not a tail scenario — it is the modal outcome in the bull case. Core earnings recovery from the trough is intact, providing a floor under the thesis even if LIDE timing slips. ~~The stock trades at a single-digit EV/EBIT on FY2026 base estimates, implying the market is pricing in very little LIDE optionality. That is a structurally mispriced situation if the technology is as mature as management represents.~~ ==At roughly EUR 24.80 and about EUR 606 M market cap on FY2025 EUR 115.3 M revenue and break-even adjusted EBIT, the stock already prices substantial LIDE optionality, but a confirmed Tier-1 design win would re-rate the multiple onto a revenue trajectory step-changed from the FY2026 EUR 105-120 M guided base.== ~~German SDAX re-rating dynamics amplify the move:~~ ==German micro-cap dynamics amplify the move post-SDAX-exit in December 2025:== thin liquidity means a concentrated buy-in from one European deep-value fund compresses the float meaningfully.

**Bear.** LIDE has been "in commercial discussions" since at least 2023; three years without a disclosed volume order is a pattern, not a data point. Glass substrate adoption for advanced packaging competes against both organic substrate incumbents and alternative glass processing approaches from DISCO and others. LPKF's core PCB prototyping segment faces secular pressure from cloud-based PCB design tools and lower-cost Asian competitors. ~~The Vitrion partnership structure adds execution risk and dilutes LPKF's direct customer relationship visibility.~~ ==Concentration of LIDE production capacity in the single Vitrion glass-foundry leaves the programme exposed to site-level execution risk during customer qualification ramps.== German small-cap illiquidity works against the holder in a risk-off environment. And the restructuring, while operationally complete, leaves a management team with limited bandwidth to simultaneously defend the core franchise and commercialise an entirely new technology in one of the most demanding customer qualification environments — semiconductor advanced packaging — in the industrial supply chain.

The asymmetry, in brief: LIDE success is worth multiples of current market capitalisation and is not in the price; ~~LIDE delay is approximately priced in on the core-business multiple, meaning the downside from further deferral is contained.~~ ==LIDE delay carries meaningful downside, because the EUR 606 M market cap on FY2025 EUR 115.3 M revenue and EUR 0.8 M adjusted EBIT already requires LIDE to deliver to justify the multiple.== The next twelve months narrow that asymmetry — or spring it.

chapters.title: LIDE inflection, core segment recovery, 2026-2030 horizon
chapters.body:
## The geometry of a bet

By the spring of 2026, LPKF Laser & Electronics had spent the better part of two years compressing itself. The operational restructuring that ran through 2023 and into 2024 was, by management's own framing, a deliberate reduction in surface area — headcount trimmed, product lines rationalised, capital redirected toward the segments most likely to generate sustainable margin. What emerged from that process was a leaner version of a company that had always lived at the niche end of precision laser systems: perhaps €100–150 million in annual revenue, listed on Frankfurt Xetra under LPK.DE ~~as an SDAX member~~ ==having spent a single year in SDAX between December 2024 and December 2025 before its index removal==, headquartered in Garbsen on the outskirts of Hannover. The machinery was running again. The question the market was pricing, somewhat uncomfortably, was whether LPKF had timed the arrival of its strategic optionality correctly.

That optionality had a name: LIDE, for Laser Induced Deep Etching. The technology, developed inside LPKF and ~~subsequently ring-fenced into a dedicated commercial vehicle~~ ==operated through a dedicated in-house center of excellence and foundry service==, used ultrashort-pulse laser sources to create high-aspect-ratio through-holes and channels in glass with a precision and throughput that conventional mechanical and chemical processes could not replicate at scale. In isolation, that was a useful industrial capability. In the context of the semiconductor industry's mid-decade search for advanced packaging substrates, it was something more charged — a positioned option on one of the few structural material transitions the chip industry had considered in twenty years.

## Glass substrates and the packaging inflection

The substrate question mattered because organic laminates — the material foundation of almost every processor package for four decades — were beginning to hit physical limits relevant to the chiplet era. As leading-edge logic disaggregated into multi-die assemblies, the density of interconnects required between dies began to press against what organic could tolerably accommodate: warpage, co-planarity tolerances, and the coefficient of thermal expansion mismatch between silicon and laminate all became more consequential as feature pitches tightened. Glass offered a different profile. Its thermal expansion coefficient sat closer to silicon's, its surface planarity was superior, and its electrical properties — lower dielectric loss at the frequencies advanced interconnects demanded — were genuinely attractive. The catch was manufacturability: drilling, etching, and metallising glass at the dimensional tolerances chip packaging required was hard, and the tooling ecosystem barely existed.

[LPKF investor relations](https://www.lpkf.com/en/investor-relations) had described LIDE as positioned for precisely this gap. The process sequence it enabled — ultrafast laser modification of glass followed by selective chemical etching, creating vertical features with aspect ratios previously associated only with silicon MEMS fabrication — was one of the credible approaches to making glass substrates manufacturable at volume. Whether the industry would adopt glass substrates broadly, and whether it would adopt them on a timeline that matched LPKF's commercial planning horizon, remained open questions as of the May 2026 snapshot. But the directional logic was not disputed: Intel had published extensively on its Glass Substrate initiative, Taiwan's advanced packaging ecosystem was evaluating the material seriously, and several leading-edge memory and logic roadmaps pointed toward glass as a plausible next-generation foundation for the highest-density assemblies.

For a company of LPKF's size, the asymmetry was notable. A glass substrate tooling market that achieved even a fraction of the scale that organic substrate tooling had reached would represent a revenue opportunity many times the company's then-current turnover. The risk, symmetrically, was that the transition would prove slower, more technically contested, or more dominated by incumbent equipment makers than the LIDE framing assumed.

## Vitrion and the commercialisation structure

~~The vehicle LPKF constructed to bring LIDE to market was Vitrion — a partnership and commercial entity designed to separate~~ ==The structure LPKF built around LIDE was Vitrion, its in-house glass-processing center of excellence and foundry service, intended to separate== the glass substrate opportunity from the operating cadence of the four legacy segments, giving it a dedicated go-to-market path and allowing semiconductor customers to engage with ~~a partner whose entire focus was glass processing rather than a subsidiary of a PCB prototyping equipment company~~ ==a clearly demarcated glass-processing operation inside LPKF rather than a buried line item inside a PCB prototyping equipment supplier==. The strategic logic was sound: semiconductor procurement relationships are long in development and specific in their technical requirements, and ~~a standalone entity~~ ==a visibly named center of excellence== could build credibility with advanced packaging customers more efficiently than ~~an embedded business unit~~ ==a less-distinguished internal team==.

As of the frozen snapshot, Vitrion had not yet generated the kind of customer disclosure or revenue recognition that would allow outside observers to assess whether the glass substrate thesis was translating into committed volume. What the ~~partnership structure~~ ==center-of-excellence structure== signalled was that LPKF's management, led by CEO Klaus Fiedler, was serious enough about the opportunity to make it structurally distinct — not a line item in the Electronics segment's quarterly update, but a separately narrated strategic asset.

## Core segments: the floor under the option

The optionality framing was sustainable only if the core business provided a stable earnings base. Here the post-restructuring picture was more legible, if not uniformly encouraging.

The Development segment — PCB prototyping systems sold to electronics manufacturers, research institutions, and engineering teams that needed rapid-iteration circuit boards — had long been LPKF's most durable franchise. The company's prototyping equipment occupied a near-monopoly position in several sub-niches; no serious competitor had dislodged it at the precision end of the market. Volume was modest and the growth ceiling was limited by the size of the addressable prototyping population, but the revenue was recurring in character and not heavily cyclical.

The Electronics segment, which housed the laser direct structuring (LDS) technology for three-dimensional molded interconnect devices, was more exposed to consumer electronics demand. LDS-enabled antennas — the technology that allowed antenna structures to be laser-activated directly onto injection-moulded plastic surfaces — had become a meaningful presence in smartphone and IoT device manufacturing. The segment's performance tracked, with a lag, the capex cycles of the consumer electronics supply chain, and the 2023-2024 downturn in handset demand had been felt. Recovery through 2025 and into 2026 was visible, though the Electronics segment faced its own competitive pressure from Asian laser system makers that had progressively narrowed the capability gap.

The Solar segment, which provided laser processing equipment for cell manufacturers, sat in a more complicated position. European solar manufacturing had not recovered the strategic momentum that policymakers had periodically promised it, and the Chinese dominance of cell production capacity had continued to concentrate purchasing decisions in a geography where LPKF's pricing position was under persistent pressure. The segment was not viewed as a core growth driver for the 2026-2030 horizon.

Welding — laser plastic welding systems sold primarily to automotive and medical device manufacturers — ~~provided a steadier contribution~~ ==was, by contrast, running at an adjusted EBIT loss of roughly EUR 4.8 million on EUR 18.6 million of revenue in 2024==. The automotive transition toward electrification had created mixed signals: some traditional plastic assembly applications declined as vehicle architectures changed, but EV battery housings and power electronics enclosures introduced new welding opportunities at different material specifications. The segment was not expected to generate headline growth, ~~but its margin profile was defensible~~ ==and its margin profile remained underwater rather than defensible as of the latest disclosed year==.

## The 2026-2030 posture

The strategic posture LPKF carried into the second half of the 2020s could be read as a two-phase construction. Phase one was the consolidation already underway: operating expenditure discipline, segment focus, and the gradual recovery of Electronics ~~and Welding~~ demand as the 2023-2024 downturn cycled through. Phase two — the one that justified the multiple the market was assigning to the equity — was contingent on LIDE and Vitrion converting the glass substrate thesis into disclosed customer engagements and, eventually, recurring system sales.

The timing uncertainty around phase two was the central analytical variable. Glass substrate adoption at volume required not only that chipmakers choose glass over organic, but that their foundry and OSAT partners invest in the tooling and process qualification at scale — a decision with a multi-year capital commitment horizon. If the industry moved toward glass substrates in the 2027-2028 window, LPKF and Vitrion would be positioned to participate in the early equipment orders. If the transition stalled at pilot-line volumes through the end of the decade, the company would need the core segments to carry more of the earnings burden than the current trajectory comfortably supported.

What LPKF had assembled, by the May 2026 snapshot, was a business that had survived its restructuring with its principal technologies intact, had ~~ring-fenced~~ ==positioned== its most consequential strategic bet in a form that semiconductor customers could engage with seriously, and retained sufficient balance sheet flexibility to sustain the development investment that LIDE commercialisation required. The question the 2026-2030 horizon posed was not whether the glass substrate opportunity was real — the physics and the industry's directional statements made that reasonably clear — but whether a €100-million-scale German laser systems specialist could capture enough of it, fast enough, to grow into the valuation that the LIDE option implied.

## Glossary

**LIDE** — Laser Induced Deep Etching; LPKF's proprietary glass processing technology enabling precision through-glass vias for semiconductor advanced packaging applications, ==supporting panels and substrates up to 515 mm x 510 mm==.

**LDS** — Laser Direct Structuring; technology for creating three-dimensional circuit traces on molded interconnect devices, widely used in smartphone antennae and automotive electronics.

**Glass core substrate** — Next-generation semiconductor packaging substrate using glass rather than organic laminate, offering superior flatness, thermal stability, and high-density via routing; primary addressable market for LIDE.

**SDAX** — Small-cap segment of the Frankfurt Stock Exchange~~, in which LPK.DE is a constituent~~ ==(LPK.DE was a constituent from 2024-12-27 to 2025-12-22)==.
